text: Uses the previously developed mKdV and Zakharov–Shabat hierarchies, resolvent recursion relations and variational string equations. The simplest undeformed equation is 2f''−f³+xf=0; integrating the boost equation introduces q.

Reviews supergravity stationary-point analysis, nonperturbative gaugino-condensation contributions to the superpotential, and sequential integration of Kaluza–Klein modes, complex-structure/dilaton modes and the radial modulus. These are effective-field-theory constructions whose quantum-gravity interpretation is questioned.

Uses Coleman–De Luccia semiclassical decay geometries and a quantum-mechanical toy potential to examine instabilities; uses renormalization-group reasoning and rough ensemble counts to assess anthropic phenomenology and supersymmetry preferences.

Infer the D7 gauge-flux energy's volume dependence by metric scaling. Expand the D7 Chern–Simons coupling to obtain B∧F, dualize B to the axion, and use gauge invariance and supersymmetry to identify the field-dependent FI term.
Analyze the 4D F-term potential using Kähler covariant derivatives and no-scale cancellation, then combine the flux constant W0 with W_np = A exp(−aT). Study extrema after adding a positive D-term.

Diagonal slicing turns a 3d partition into an interlacing sequence of ordinary partitions. A complex-fermion Fock-space representation and bosonized Γ± transfer operators evaluate the weighted partition sum; their commutation factors recover the MacMahon product.

Skew Schur functions, the Jacobi–Trudy determinant, transposition identities and Littlewood–Richardson coefficients convert transfer-matrix expressions into the topological-vertex formula expressed through Chern–Simons Hopf-link data.

For general dimers, homology-weighted torus configurations define the Kasteleyn spectral polynomial F. Imported dimer results identify surface tension with the Legendre dual of its Ronkin function; the Wulff construction supplies a limit shape for the corresponding boundary conditions.

The two-loop calculation uses dimensional regularization with ε = 3−D and evaluates simple-pole residues in three dimensions. The paper acknowledges Chern–Simons tensor difficulties and relates poles to logarithms in an exponential-cutoff scheme.

Field equations and field redefinitions remove redundant counterterms. In the example, only two dimension-four matter operators are essential; the calculation separates gravity-induced contributions from four-fermion self-renormalization and subtracts fermion wave-function renormalization.

Dimensional grading gives βiI = ΣJ γiIJ(α)λiJ + δiI, where δ depends polynomially on lower-level irrelevant couplings and is at least quadratic in them. Finiteness becomes a sequence of linear systems.

The probe Born–Infeld plus Wess–Zumino action is reduced in static gauge. Conserved energy, parallel momentum and angular momentum reduce the rigid relativistic motion to radial/orbital quadratures; elementary and elliptic integrals arise for specified dimensions.

Orientifold interactions are computed from the Möbius-strip amplitude: its small-modulus limit gives massless closed-string exchange, while the large-modulus/open-string description gives a short-distance expansion. The proposed Lorentzian potential is an interpolation between asymptotics.

For Born–Infeld-only motion, equivalent nonrelativistic potentials are V_eq = −k_δ/r^(7−p), δ = p−p′. Identifications are k_2 = (ε²−u_i²)k/2, k_4 = (ε²−u_i²−1)k/2 and ε_eq = (ε²−u_i²−1)/2. The quantum discussion squares the formal Hamiltonian equation.

A BPS-like rewriting organizes the action into geometric, flux and gauge squares, together with additional curvature and dΣ terms. Vanishing squares supplies candidate background conditions, but the residual term must also have vanishing variation before equations of motion follow.

The geometric analysis uses the Lee form, Nijenhuis tensor, Bismut connection and torsionful curvatures. The identity R⁺_ab cd = R⁻_cd ab − (dH)_abcd translates conditions on R⁺ base indices into R⁻ fiber-index conditions to the stated perturbative order.

The proposed microscopic superpotential is compared schematically with c + e^(−S), then inserted into the four-dimensional N = 1 F-term potential using a tree-level Kähler potential to test a no-scale interpretation.

Trace over the invisible Rindler wedge to obtain the thermal vacuum state ρ_R0 and the excited state ρ_R1. Compute background-subtracted energy and entropy, regulating each state first and then subtracting before removing the cutoff.

Free-field calculations use Minkowski/Rindler Bogoliubov transformations and Fock-space traces. The appendix motivates the large-n entropy expansion through moments Tr ρ^(1+ε), subsystem combinatorics for integer moments and continuation toward ε = 0.
Expand entropy to first order in δρ = ρ_R1−ρ_R0. Tr δρ = 0 and ρ_R0 proportional to exp(−H/T) give δS ≈ −Tr(δρ ln ρ_R0) = δE/T. The authors supplement this with equilibrium thermodynamic reasoning.

Duality chasing relates M/F-theory flux backgrounds to IIB orientifolds, then through two T-dualities and S-duality to heterotic backgrounds. Matching brane harmonic functions to flux warp factors supplies an alternative description using NS5 branes.
Methods include recursive algebraic expansion of the anomaly equation, twisted Dolbeault/sheaf cohomology and Bismut's index theorem, and a target-space six-dimensional Dirac index for chirality.

Kaluza–Klein reduction recasts three-dimensional backreaction as two-dimensional dilaton gravity. For nonzero gauge flux the potential is V(Φ)=2/Φ³; boost and null-boost instead have vanishing flux. Dilaton-independent conformal shock matter permits exact nonlinear solutions.

Construct invariant Klein–Gordon modes by averaging covering-space plane waves and Fourier projecting along the orbifold isometry. Separation of variables produces imaginary-order Bessel modes for shifted boosts and Airy modes for the O-plane.

Tree amplitudes use the covering-theory inheritance principle for nonwinding external string states, with Faddeev–Popov removal of continuous-orbit overcounting. Winding-state equations reduce to confluent hypergeometric equations.
Evaluate DBI and Wess–Zumino actions in source-brane fields; use conserved energy and angular momentum, orbital quadratures, and a radial effective potential to identify probe turning points.

Israel junction conditions give the boundary-brane equation H² = κ5⁴ρ²/36 − g(a)/a² when brane matter has no direct coupling to bulk fields besides gravity. Scale-factor evolution is recast as zero-energy motion, ȧ² + W(a) = 0, with W ≤ 0 on allowed trajectories.

For the simplest S-brane example, evolve a small massless minimally coupled scalar on the induced geometry in conformal time, using v_k = aδφ_k. The displayed mode analysis uses WKB expressions away from k² = 1.

Dimensional reduction of the flux–gaugino perfect square is expressed through four-dimensional N=1 supergravity. For one Kähler modulus, K contains −log(S+S̄)−3log(T+T̄) and the complex-structure term; W/μ³=2h/c−C_H exp[−8π²f_hidden/C_H]. Stabilization uses Kähler-covariant derivatives of W.

Explicit mathematical tools include representations π1(Q)→G for Chern–Simons values, a cohomological exact sequence for the global worldsheet anomaly, and index theorems for virtual dimensions of fractional-instanton moduli spaces.

Solve the matter-scalar constraint using symmetric G and antisymmetric B, and differentiate with respect to the 36 independent entries of P=G+B. At G=I, B=0 the matter kinetic term is −(1/2)∂Pab∂Pab, so the matter Hessian is the canonically normalized scalar mass-squared matrix there.

Separate the potential as V=Σij[R^(ij)(φ)Vij(Z)+I^(ij)Wij(Z)], with Vij symmetric and Wij antisymmetric. Extremize the SU(1,1) sector analytically, then evaluate matter derivatives using the gauge-factor structure constants at the matter origin.

Estimate vacuum decay using an SO(4)-symmetric zero-temperature instanton and dimensional scaling of the radion kinetic term and potential. A footnote reports an additional detailed calculation agreeing with the estimate.

Integrate auxiliary fields through a path-integral treatment. A functional delta, represented by a quadratic field-strength term with ξ → 0, enforces closed connections while retaining global information that naive substitution of equations of motion would lose.

Use the one-loop Casimir potential as a function of radion size and SS flux. The paper imports the massive-hypermultiplet kernel and uses an exponential approximation F(x) = e^(−2x)(3 + 6x + 6x² + 4x³), supplemented by numerical plots and truncated Fourier sums.

Estimate probe backreaction using boosted-source and domain-wall gravitational arguments, production through the adiabatic parameter ω̇/ω², and stability through linear scalar perturbations about the rolling solutions.

Use the DBI action to resum finite-velocity higher-derivative terms from virtual open strings at planar order. This action does not itself include on-shell W/string production or closed-string loops; these require separate estimates.

Solve homogeneous cosmological dynamics through a Hamilton–Jacobi formulation with H = H(φ), then determine φ(t) and a(t). This assumes monotonic φ and a single-valued H(φ), excluding scalar oscillations from that formulation.

The fluctuation calculation uses a linear convolution from initial fractal-density fluctuations to interstitial-black-hole density, Fourier-space correlations, and conformal scaling of a double time integral. It replaces the earlier field-theory calculation around the p=rho background.

Israel-junction geometry continuity is applied using equal-area slicing. For an isolated radiation-filled sphere, t R(t)^2=t^(2/3)L^2 implies R(t) proportional to t^(-1/6), motivating a more complicated initial normal region.

The imported isolated-horizon Hamiltonian framework makes the first law necessary and sufficient for Hamiltonian evolution. Horizon energies and masses are obtained by choosing surface-gravity normalization and integration constants, then integrating horizon first laws.

Canonical Euclidean comparison chooses one horizon as boundary and makes the other regular, adding one quarter of its area to the action. Generally unequal horizon temperatures permit equilibrium with only one horizon in this construction.
Expand the D3 tension and four-form coupling for slowly varying radial motion. The resulting potential is V = T3(Ω̂1⁴ − ω), with canonical field defined by dφ = √T3 Ω̂1Ω̂2 dr.

Use radial type IIB supergravity equations and their constraint, expanding to O(P²) around KW or O(H²) around KT. In the latter calculation, a decoupled first-order equation determines the relevant potential derivative.
Taylor-expand the local background in transverse coordinates, insert it into bosonic DBI–CS and fermionic brane actions, and project invariant fields for orbifolds.
Use N=1 supergravity with W proportional to ∫G3∧Ω: (3,0), (0,3), and primitive (1,2) fluxes correspond respectively to dilaton, overall Kähler, and complex-structure auxiliaries.

The proposed D-string identification is tested by matching brane and soliton tensions and by dualizing the RR two-form into an axion whose gauge-covariant gradient reproduces the long-range RR energy.

Bogomol'nyi completion includes Einstein curvature and Gibbons–Hawking boundary terms. Matter and gravitino BPS conditions remove bulk contributions, leaving the string energy determined by the difference of radial boundary terms.

Set the chiral-fermion, gaugino, and gravitino variations to zero using a spinor projection. The resulting first-order equations include F12=±D and the gravitino condition 1-C'(r)=±A_theta^B, with correlated sign choices.

Tracks the expansion of an initial Hubble patch through inflation and reheating, estimates its radiation entropy at the beginning of radiation domination, and compares that entropy with the proposed ceiling. Subsequent standard evolution is treated as conserving the patch's total entropy.

Uses Bousso's imported D-bound, S_D=(A₀−A)/(4G), where A₀ is the pure de Sitter horizon area and A the horizon area with matter present. At radiation onset the author approximates this ceiling by S_D∼Λ₀⁻¹.

Imports fluid thermodynamics for p=κρ, with entropy density scaling as ρ^(1/(1+κ)), and the four-dimensional cavity collapse threshold S_R∼R^[3−2/(1+κ)]. The cavity radius is identified with the de Sitter cosmological horizon.

An Omega-background localizes the gauge path integral to invariant instantons at toric vertices and connecting spheres. Noncommutative coordinates regularize pointlike U(1) configurations; fluctuation determinants and equivariant index formulas produce vertex and edge factors.

Geometric quantization identifies holomorphic sections with integral points of a toric moment polytope: p_i=N_i gs and t_a=m_a gs. Closure under multiplication by coordinate monomials converts allowed section spaces into monomial ideals and three-dimensional partitions.

For general X, the formulation passes to moduli of ideal sheaves. Singular moduli spaces require virtual fundamental classes rather than naive integration; the Donaldson–Thomas class is identified as the mathematical integration object.

Bottom-up model building uses combined geometric and Chan–Paton orbifold projections, quiver spectra, twisted RR tadpole cancellation, and Green–Schwarz couplings to determine gauge factors, chiral matter, and massive U(1) combinations.
Geometric cycle deformations, SL(2,Z) monodromies of elliptic-fiber one-cycles, and junction/prong creation provide the appendix’s argument for homology constraints on permissible flux assignments.

Moduli potentials are organized through the flux superpotential W=∫G3∧Ω, no-scale supergravity, twisted-modulus Fayet–Iliopoulos D-terms, flux-induced charged-scalar masses, and proposed nonperturbative gauge effects.

Obtain Killing prepotentials from the quaternionic SU(2) connection, construct the superpotential and scalar potential, and analyze critical points and Hessians. Coordinates ρ=sinh(r)cos(θ), η=cosh(r)sin(θ) regularize the two BPS fixed points.

Construct the target metric from F(ρ,η), satisfying ρ²(∂ρ²+∂η²)F=(3/4)F. The paper discusses modular eigenfunctions and Eisenstein-series instanton interpretations, then uses a finite three-pole solution.

Kibble production and tachyon vacuum-manifold topology distinguish strings formed at brane annihilation from possible higher-energy defects. With a surviving D3-brane, the relevant vacuum manifold remains S³ and does not support Kibble production of stable D-strings.

Two-form gauge invariance, brane U(1) flux, and Chern–Simons couplings track charge continuity when strings acquire endpoints. Integrating bulk RR fields over compact cycles identifies four-dimensional gauge fields and wrapped-D3 baryon vertices.

Decay estimates use Euclidean world-sheet holes and the Schwinger-type exponent B = πσ²/ρ, with σ the boundary action per length and ρ the removed world-sheet action per area. The same framework treats baryon-pair-mediated transitions.

Linear scalar perturbations in longitudinal gauge determine π–gravity mixing and propagators. Retarded Fourier integrals treat a source switched on at finite time; de Sitter equations and stationary numerical examples examine modulation, screening, and source-history dependence.

Taylor expansion about a fixed background yields finitely many coefficients at each derivative order. Nonrelativistic power counting uses E→sE, x→s⁻¹ᐟ²x, π→s¹ᐟ⁴π; the leading cubic interaction scales as s¹ᐟ⁴ and is irrelevant in the infrared.

A unitary-gauge construction uses the scalar as a clock, residual spatial diffeomorphisms, induced geometry, and extrinsic curvature. Restoring the Goldstone π exposes its kinetic terms and permits a nonlinear effective action.

Perturbations are converted through the position-dependent end time of inflation. The appendix tests reheating matching with Israel junction conditions, assuming reheating much shorter than H⁻¹ and nonsingular spatial stress components.

The three-point function is evaluated at first order in the interaction using an in-in commutator integral. The early-time contour selects the interacting vacuum; contour rotation gives exponential convergence for numerical evaluation of momentum configurations.

Nonrelativistic power counting assigns π scaling dimension 1/4 and estimates frozen fluctuations. Quantization of the de Sitter mode equation, conversion to conformal time, and a Hankel-function solution with a short-wavelength flat-space limit give the scalar spectrum.

Use symmetry-selected periods inherited from mirror calculations, transform Picard–Fuchs period bases to symplectic bases, and expand near ψ=0. Sen’s F-theory orientifold construction supplies the geometries and D3-charge budgets.

For model A, approximate irrational supersymmetry requirements by rational flux ratios, solve the supersymmetry equations through O(ψ²), then perturb ψ and τ to solve their covariant-derivative equations through O(ψ⁴), where a nonzero superpotential appears.

Solve fixed-point conditions and evaluate the stability matrix; obtain an analytic reduced flow at vanishing cosmological constant. Integrate the two-coupling flow with tuned initial conditions to identify the separatrix connecting ultraviolet and Gaussian fixed points.

Project the exact renormalisation-group flow onto the two retained operators using background-field regulators. The scalar regulator is optimized as Ropt(q) = (k² − q²)θ(k² − q²). The authors report computations for arbitrary dimension and gauge parameter α.

Use Liouville OPEs, minimal-model fusion rules and Chebyshev identities to formulate ring multiplication modulo BRST commutators. Disk one-point functions motivate boundary-state identifications and test the ring ansatz; ring action computes sphere correlators with three tachyons.

Extract algebraic curves from derivatives of FZZT disk amplitudes; study uniformization, singularities F = dF = 0 and contour periods. Compare these data with matrix resolvents and analyze polynomial deformations that preserve singularities.

Use consistent gauged-supergravity reductions, symmetric gauge configurations and radial warp-factor equations. Self-dual one-boundary fillings supply explicit comparison configurations for the meron example.
Compute bulk-to-boundary kernels and quotient-image sums for correlators while neglecting interior interactions. The image sum converges for Δ>d−1; interacting correlators need not equal image sums.

Study quadratic fluctuations with normalizability at both ends, using hypergeometric scalar solutions and numerical radial node tests; compare renormalized on-shell actions including boundary counterterms.

Use binary polyhedral group inclusions to reduce the dodecahedral supersymmetry question to Q8={±1,±i,±j,±k}; represent its generators by quaternion multiplication on the four spatial embedding coordinates.

Apply the group generators to an imported explicit AdS5 Killing-spinor expression and impose simultaneous invariance. For lens-space actions, test the resulting constant-spinor constraint through its stated matrix eigenvalues.

Use dimensional reduction and truncation: reduce on T6 and retain SU(3) singlets to obtain an N=1 toy action. In heterotic M-theory, include the leading internal-coordinate dependence and average over the Calabi–Yau manifold and the eleventh-dimensional interval.

Insert the gaugino bilinear directly into auxiliary fields inferred from supersymmetry transformations, then minimize the supergravity scalar potential. An alternative condensate contribution to the superpotential is reviewed as qualitatively similar but quantitatively different.

Begin with an SU(2,2|1) superconformal action and a compensating chiral multiplet Y. Gauge-fix extra conformal symmetries, choosing real Y to remain regular at W=0; gauge transformations of Y generate constant contributions to Killing potentials.

Compute inflationary corrections using supertraces of field-dependent masses. Analyze string modes with the transverse Dirac equation and index arguments, then use projected residual supersymmetry transformations to examine boson–fermion pairing.
Apply the imported Hwang–Noh f(R,φ,X) perturbation formalism and slow-roll approximations to estimate curvature and tensor spectra, spectral indices, and their comparison with observational contours.
Motivate the Born–Infeld effective action through leading terms of a four-massive-scalar disk amplitude; introduce massless closed-string couplings using covariance and T-duality.
Numerically integrate homogeneous evolution through inflation and oscillations, and separately evolve Fourier modes of field fluctuations to examine their behavior.

Construct the N=1 F-term potential from flux and condensate superpotentials. Heterotic threshold corrections introduce gauge functions f_i=S+β_iT; multiple condensates supply additional adjustable exponential terms.

Expand holomorphic W locally through cubic order to evaluate the potential, stationarity equations, and Hessian. The one-field mixed-curvature diagnostic needs only quadratic terms; Mathematica supplies symbolic manipulation, followed by explicit two-field examples.

At fixed ρ, a randomized search minimizes the potential on the symmetric locus using Mathematica FindMinimum with a modified Powell method. Relatively prime flux choices have the stated cutoff a,b,c,d≤10, with 50 attempts per choice. Candidates are then examined using derivatives of the full real-metric and axiodilaton potential.

The authors dimensionally reduce the ten-dimensional type IIB component action and evaluate the resulting four-dimensional Einstein-frame potential. This bypasses the problematic naive application of the usual no-scale Kähler-potential/superpotential description to the torus.

Semiclassical backreaction couples classical φ to quantum χ mode equations and a subtracted ⟨χ²⟩. Numerical integration discretizes the momentum integral; an adiabatic expansion with iterative backreaction treats the early, weakly nonadiabatic passage.

In/out Bogoliubov transformations, scattering through an inverted parabolic potential, and complex-time WKB give nk=exp[−π(k²+g²μ²)/(gv)] for the prescribed straight trajectory. The paper acknowledges substantial overlap with established particle-production and preheating techniques.

Kaluza–Klein mode expansions, explicit smooth transition functions, and Dirac indices illustrate changing massless modes. Covariantly constant adjoint sections identify the actual unbroken gauge generators at the endpoints.

Positive two-term monads convert Chern-class constraints into integer equations. The appendix's finiteness argument uses S≤B, M≤min(B/2,B−n), and mmax≤B−2(M−1), with fixed B and finite rank, to bound the allowed monad data.

For brane recombination, a change of complex structure turns special Lagrangian two-cycles in T4 into holomorphic curves. Cubic embeddings of the elliptic factors in P2 × P2 allow orientifold-invariant (2,2) divisor deformations; the authors calculate genus 37 for a generic curve.

Construct the N=1 supergravity F- and D-term potential from a cubic matter superpotential plus WOM=h exp(−T) and WGC=g exp[−(S−γT)/CH], where γ=GvL and CH is the hidden gauge group's dual Coxeter number.

Retain leading terms in the matter and inverse-volume expansions; extremize axionic phases, use charged-matter stationarity and its contraction with C, and solve the remaining transcendental L-extremization equation numerically. A simpler exponential-balancing equation estimates the minimum's location.

Classify intrinsic torsion through dJ and dΩ and the five SU(3) torsion classes. Combine these relations with flux Bianchi identities and the ten-dimensional form-field equations of motion to constrain flux components and warp factors.

Set the string-frame gravitino and dilatino supersymmetry variations to zero. Decompose the ten-dimensional Killing spinor into external and internal factors, impose SU(3)-singlet projectors, and separate the resulting equations by internal chirality and external spinor structure.

The cosmological test combines horizon growth with ρ∝R^−3(1+w). The local test compares an assumed repulsive force F(L)∼Λ(L)L with the Sun's attraction M⊙/L2, using a conservative inequality rather than a detailed planetary-data fit.

A perturbative backreaction diagnostic uses connected, non-1PI vacuum-bubble graphs joined by gravitons. With g graviton lines, the stated scaling is M4(M4L2)^g, indicating a large correction for L>M^−2 and motivating a background-metric shift.

Ultraviolet mode counting relates the zero-point estimate Λqm∼M4 to s∼M3, giving Λqm∼s^(4/3). The argument concerns scaling estimates rather than an exact quantum-gravity calculation or a specified numerical prefactor.

The symbolic workflow computes the scalar metric, Kähler-covariant derivatives DiW, and F- and D-term potentials from user inputs. It supports searching for constant supersymmetric configurations through DiW=0, splitting complex fields into real components, and plotting two-field sections while holding other fields fixed.

The numerical workflow uses canonical momenta Pi=a^3 Gij phi_dot^j and a Hamiltonian first-order formulation. Scalar coordinates and momenta are evolved together with the scale factor and Hubble parameter. Initial scalar data are specified, while the initial Hubble parameter is obtained from the Friedmann first integral.

Superspace and component chiral–linear duality derive the otherwise implicit Kähler coordinates. Cubic homogeneity in the linear variables exposes the no-scale cancellation, while differentiation of implicit coordinate relations determines the metric.

Kaluza–Klein reduction expands surviving fields in harmonic forms and integrates the ten-dimensional action over Y. F5 self-duality is imposed through equations of motion, eliminating half the potentials; a Weyl rescaling gives the four-dimensional Einstein normalization.

Estimate scalar perturbations using a multifield expression involving derivatives of the expansion N, reportedly approximated well by a field-velocity expression in these examples; impose the historical COBE amplitude normalization.

Construct a four-dimensional supergravity sector with r=T+T*−k(φ,φ*), logarithmic Kähler dependence, f=f0+αB, and nonperturbative superpotential terms Ae^(−aT)+CQ^ℓe^(−cB), supplemented by antibrane terms.

Numerically integrate the full coupled scalar and FRW equations with the noncanonical Kähler metric, using the scale factor as time variable. Slow-roll diagnostics use the covariant potential Hessian and its metric-weighted eigenvalues.

The future-horizon integral and Friedmann equation are rewritten using ΩΛ and x=ln a, then differentiated into an evolution equation. The author states exact solvability for arbitrary c, displays the c=1 implicit solution, and extracts early- and late-time asymptotics.

Conformal coordinates with a finite upper time limit recast the horizon as r=−η and Rh=a|η|. A second-order expansion of ln ρΛ around a=1 supplies the reported low-redshift equation-of-state parameterization.

Construct Dirac-spinor generators using Clifford matrices satisfying {ΓI,ΓJ}=2ηIJ, with blocks assigned to the two observer sectors; organize the resulting Fock tensor products into de Sitter representations and extract singlets.

Reinterpret antipodal tensor-product states as processes: the first factor supplies incoming kets, while the second supplies outgoing bras after charge, time and parity reversal. Invariant tensor pairings then supply S-matrix amplitudes.

Wess–Zumino consistency and Stora–Zumino descent classify consistent anomalies modulo local counterterms. Orbifold projectors inserted into covering-space traces separate untwisted and fixed-point sectors.

Fujikawa measure Jacobians are defined with a Gaussian heat-kernel regulator and evaluated through supersymmetric quantum mechanics in the β → 0 limit. Normal-coordinate expansion retains quadratic fluctuations; determinants use ζ-function regularization.

Integrate the time-symmetric Einstein constraint to obtain the mass function; minimize configuration energy over exterior scalar profiles with fixed core and cutoff data. Static scalar-hair black holes provide the cutoff comparison configurations.

Evolve homogeneous hyperbolic FRW cosmologies numerically, trace radial null congruences, and use Raychaudhuri focusing to strengthen lower bounds on the horizon size required to cloak the singularity.

Lift the five-dimensional solution to ten dimensions and expand a BPS D3-brane's DBI and Wess–Zumino contributions at large radius to diagnose an instability invisible in the restricted scalar sector.

Maximally symmetric spinor parallel transport reduces the invariant fermionic two-point function to an ordinary differential equation. Its short-distance expansion is inserted into a point-split stress-tensor trace to extract the ultraviolet divergence.

The Dirac spectral problem is reduced to first-order operators Q and Q† and a factorized second-order equation. Hypergeometric scattering solutions and the reflection coefficient are quoted from the shape-invariant-potential treatment [30].

Replace the linearized warped background by the exact nonlinear solution; the former is its tangent approximation at the visible boundary. Assess effective-supergravity control through Calabi–Yau and membrane volumes and suppression of multiply wrapped instantons.

Use a dimensionally reduced four-dimensional effective potential containing open membrane instanton (OMI) and hidden-boundary gaugino condensation (GC) contributions. Their opposing dependence on orbifold length supplies the proposed stabilization mechanism.

Expand the DBI action through cubic order and evaluate the first-order interaction-Hamiltonian commutator integral for the three-point function. In the large-γ, small-ε regime, matter self-interactions dominate the non-Gaussian signal.

Apply the general noncanonical scalar-perturbation formalism to the curvature variable ζ and its rescaled mode v = zζ. Solve the mode equation using Hankel functions, including the varying sound speed when calculating the scalar tilt.

Use Hamilton–Jacobi evolution with H regarded as a function of φ and a DBI-modified first-order Friedmann equation. The reviewed massive-scalar background has power-law expansion, φ proportional to 1/t, and γ proportional to t².

Special geometry and Grassmann or Wick integrations determine densities. Dropping the determinant's absolute value gives the signed index; the authors recover the earlier formula dμ_ind=π^(−m)det(R+ω1).

Delta-function counts include absolute Jacobian determinants. Replacing the flux sum by an integral, Laplace-transforming the tadpole bound and changing to an orthonormal Hodge basis reduces counting to Gaussian integrations.

Treat S as a background and use V_T = V + F. Locate merger of the minimum and maximum through V_T′ = V_T″ = 0; in the linear approximation, V″ vanishes where the maximal zero-temperature slope balances the thermal slope. Select the largest critical temperature if multiple solutions occur.

Expand thermal free energy locally as F/T⁴ = A + B δg + O(δg²). The sign argument uses the negative order-g² coefficient and imports nonsupersymmetric perturbative results through g⁵ plus comparisons with lattice QCD.

Dimensional reduction and Weyl rescaling produce the radial-modulus potential. Power-law ansätze and an autonomous phase-plane system identify exponential-potential tracker solutions and their stability; the appendix extends earlier analyses to positive spatial curvature.

Escape is treated using imported Hawking–Moss thermal activation and Coleman–de Luccia tunneling prescriptions. The paper compares exponentially suppressed lifetimes using barrier height and bubble-wall tension; their relative magnitudes determine which process dominates.
Local period expansions determine K, metric and curvature. Truncated DτW=DψW=0 equations become a real linear system for ψ² near zero and an equation for ln(1−ψ) near the conifold.

Monte Carlo samples random integer fluxes in finite component intervals, solves the local equations and fits cumulative radial distributions and tadpole-dependent counts. Separate scans use approximately 10⁷–10¹⁰ flux choices.

For a generic confining metric ds²=dr²+f(r)dxμ², separate the bulk wave equation using K=e^{iqx}F(r). Interpret the radial spectrum as four-dimensional hadron masses and write boundary propagators with poles 1/(q²−M²).
Use D3-worldvolume Wess–Zumino couplings ∫C∧exp F and a two-R-R-field Green–Schwarz action. The CA equation of motion supplies the anomalous axial-current relation, with Jμ identified as (1/α′)∂μCA.

Represent the boundary tr F F̃ two-point function through bulk propagators of the ten-dimensional R-R axion C and twisted R-R field CA, weighted by their couplings ξ and λ. Assign their modes to pseudoscalar glueballs and flavor-singlet mesons, respectively.

Toric triangulations, intersection numbers, and Mori/Kähler cones determine divisor volumes and admissible radii. D3-instanton contributions are analyzed through vertical M5 divisors: the imported zero-mode criterion gives contributions when h0,j = 0 for j = 1,2,3; arithmetic genus one is the broader criterion used, subject to caveats below.

Flux searches start at rational large-complex-structure points, find short vectors in the lattice solving DW = 0, then restore corrections. Statistical searches replace flux sums by continuous integrals; high-dimensional densities and volumes are estimated by Monte Carlo, replacing the density by a sampled average.

Computes Chern classes through a Weierstrass model and ambient projective-bundle cohomology, then integrates over the elliptic fiber. For nonabelian sectors, additionally invokes reduction to a three-dimensional Coulomb branch and resolution of ADE fibers.
Uses Witten’s imported fermion-zero-mode criterion χ(D)=1, then Todd classes and adjunction to express it as ∫M(c₂(M)[D]²+[D]⁴)=−24. The arithmetic-genus condition is necessary, not sufficient.

Use the asymptotic positive-frequency mode exp(−ikη)/√(2k) as φ̇ → 0, Bogolyubov coefficients and a particle-production integral. Estimate the super-Hubble spectrum by slow-roll analysis and matching inflationary and radiation-era solutions.
Expand the gauge action to quadratic order in Coulomb gauge, A0 = 0 and ∇·A = 0. Introduce A_tilde,k = b^(1/2) A_k, with b = V/√(1−φ̇²), obtaining A_tilde,k″ + [k²−f(η)]A_tilde,k = 0.

Numerically evolve the background and magnetic-amplitude factor α for β = 10^−9 with initial φ̇ = 0. Analyze reheating using an approximate sub-Hubble oscillator equation and numerical mode-energy curves.

Dimensional reduction followed by a Weyl rescaling to Einstein frame exposes the coupling and volume dependence of potential terms. Stationarity equations are solved after including flux–axion couplings and compact-space charge constraints.

Flux-vacuum counting uses a bounded region in flux space. Entropy is investigated on an approximate Coulomb branch using wrapped D5/NS5 domain walls, D3-branes required by Gauss’ law, and string junctions/webs. These domain walls are generically time dependent.

Dimensional reduction and Weyl rescaling recast the bubble as a Coleman–De Luccia gravity–scalar problem. Numerical shooting varies the pinch-off parameter r0 to obtain undershoot and overshoot of the stabilized vacuum.

Geodesic motion is reduced using conserved momenta to an effective radial potential. Bounce actions include gravitational boundary terms and scalar contributions generated by reduction and Weyl rescaling; nonzero-potential flat and AdS actions are evaluated numerically.

Use annulus amplitudes and Schwinger-type products to calculate stretched-open-string pair production between strings carrying D1 charge. Light-state truncations, squeezed-state multiplicities and junction force balance then estimate actual reconnection.

Expand the warped string world-sheet action near transverse potential minima. A quadratic massive-scalar calculation with a string-scale ultraviolet cutoff gives Gaussian fluctuations and an effective overlap density replacing inverse compactification volume.

Wrap macroscopic strings on a large auxiliary torus and use the optical theorem: sphere amplitudes for F–F collisions and disk amplitudes for F–(p,q). Regge limits convert the forward absorptive amplitude into an inclusive interaction probability.

Apply the Kubo formula to the zero-momentum Txy commutator. The holographic coupling of Txy to an xy-polarized graviton relates the spectral function to its absorption cross section, giving η=σabs(0)/(16πG).

Linearize Einstein’s equations with only an x,y-independent hxy perturbation. Background equations reduce the equation for hxy/f to the minimally coupled massless-scalar equation. An imported low-frequency absorption theorem then identifies its cross section with horizon area per unit brane volume.

Set fermion variations to zero using a half-supersymmetry projector. Derive coupled first-order Higgs, gauge and gravitino equations, then analyze origin and asymptotic expansions and their free integration constants.

Use a one-loop inflaton potential, slow-roll equations and historical COBE normalization for inflationary estimates. Rough tachyonic-growth and correlation-scale arguments support a qualitative extrapolation from earlier semilocal-string simulations.

Reduce D3/D7 world-volume actions with explicit volume factors and canonically rotate fields to match the P-term model. Use F-theory Weierstrass data and seven-brane singularities to describe compact charge cancellation and enhanced symmetries.

The gravitational action is decomposed into horizon neighborhoods and a canonical bulk term. Einstein constraints and stationarity eliminate the latter; the two-dimensional Gauss–Bonnet theorem evaluates the shrinking horizon neighborhoods. A separate finite-thickness Gauss–Bonnet argument relates tension to deficit angle.

Double analytic continuation retains the periodically identified transverse Killing coordinate and continues the base manifold, producing Lorentzian braneworlds with de Sitter, Minkowski or anti-de Sitter geometry in the nonrotating construction.

For the scalar candidate, the authors couple NS-NS two-form and off-diagonal metric perturbations, linearize the Einstein equations using computer algebra, and obtain the same radial equation from a quadratic one-dimensional Papadopoulos–Tseytlin effective action.

A coupled RR three-form/five-form fluctuation ansatz reduces the linearized equations to a radial second-order ODE. The authors use homogeneous solutions and a Wronskian construction, impose infrared and ultraviolet regularity, and test convergence of three radial norm integrals.

Dualize the axion to a closed (D−1)-form, derive a scalar Bogomol’nyi bound, and reduce on-shell action expressions to boundary integrals using Stokes’ theorem. Gravitational terms require the Gibbons–Hawking term and flat-space extrinsic-curvature subtraction.

Use timelike Kaluza–Klein reduction and a scalar-field rotation to relate the Euclidean theory to Lorentzian Einstein–Maxwell–dilaton theory, with b²=a²+2(D−2)/(D−1). World-volume reductions similarly organize the p-brane uplifts and their additional dilatons.

Solve the bulk equations with ds²=e^{2B(r)}(dr²+r²dΩ²), φ=φ(r), χ=χ(r). The solution uses flat-space harmonic functions f±=1±q/r^{D−2}; a logarithm of their quotient is harmonic in the resulting conformally flat geometry.

Use a four-dimensional Kähler potential and flux, gaugino-condensate and membrane superpotentials. First solve DᵢW=0 for AdS; then analyze stationarity of U=eᴷ(G⁻¹|DW|²−3|W|²)+U_D through analytic balances and a numerical algebraic equation.

Derive anomaly constraints through descent and Chern–Simons/Green–Schwarz inflow. Obtain tension potentials by dimensional reduction of boundary and five-brane actions, using an Einstein-normalized metric and Hermitian Yang–Mills identities.

For proposed horizon modifications, use reflected null geodesics and optical volume to estimate return times, and impose normalizability with Dirichlet conditions at the wormhole’s two spatial infinities to characterize real normal frequencies.

Review the exactly solvable hypergeometric radial problem with ingoing horizon behavior and vanishing flux at AdS infinity. Its quasi-normal frequencies are compared with the real normalizable spectrum of global AdS.

Use linear response and thermal two-point functions: compute Euclidean torus correlators and analytically continue to real time. Free-fermion theta functions provide an explicit finite-size example; holographic correlators follow from bulk Dirichlet solutions and two variations of the on-shell action.

Construct the standard supergravity F-term potential, add positive uplift, and search for saddles stable along X but weakly tachyonic along Y, evaluating slow-roll curvature with the noncanonical kinetic normalization.

Numerically evolve both fields using their curved field-space metric and e-fold time N. The authors compare two scalar-power approximations during slow roll and scan parameter intervals while retuning the vacuum uplift.

Classify local stability by linearizing around critical points and examining eigenvalue real parts: all negative gives an attractor, all positive a repeller, and mixed signs a saddle. Numerically integrate interpolating solutions to illustrate the resulting phase portraits and acceleration intervals.

Organize the algebra by R=rank(α), using the row Gram matrix A_ij=α_i·α_j. For R=m invert A and retained-subset matrices; for R<m use the invertible column Gram matrix B_IJ and separately enforce coupling relations and dependent-y constraints.

Rewrite the equations as an autonomous system in Hubble-normalized variables with evolution parameter ln(a). The Friedmann constraint is x²+y²=1, acceleration requires x²<1/3, and stationary variables give power laws with p=1/(3x²), or de Sitter behavior when x²=0.

Warped dimensional reduction determines the lower-dimensional gravitational coupling. Graviton and scalar wave equations are reduced to a Schrödinger problem with a Pöschl–Teller potential, distinguishing normalizable bound states from the continuum.

A stretched-horizon diffusion formula and dissipative horizon boundary conditions probe hydrodynamics. Keeping only radial metric dependence in a locally flat region gives D=R for d=5; d>5 remains finite, while d=4 is logarithmically divergent.

The authors expand probe DBI actions in derivatives and thermal corrections, comparing protected zero-temperature interactions with thermal expectation values. Curved dS slices introduce curvature couplings and T²/E² corrections, whereas the flat thermal example has a T⁴/E⁴ expansion.
Use the Leray spectral sequence for divisors Dᵢ→S with P¹ fibers to obtain Hⁱ,⁰(Dᵢ)≃Hⁱ,⁰(S), hence χ(Dᵢ)=h⁰,⁰(S)−h¹,⁰(S)+h²,⁰(S).

Describe K3 complex structures by oriented spacelike two-planes in the signature-(3,19) cohomology lattice. ADE enhancement is identified through norm −2 roots orthogonal to both the complex-structure plane and the elliptic U sublattice; heterotic Wilson lines locate the SO(8)⁴ point.
Test stabilization by deforming complex structures and checking whether fixed G₄ remains of type (2,2). Compute D7 displacement dependence using the flux superpotential W=∫G₄∧Ω₄.

Reduces the RR fluctuation equations to an inhomogeneous radial second-order ODE and applies variation of parameters with a Wronskian. The correction retains the KS homogeneous solutions [sinh(2τ)−2τ]^(1/3) and [sinh(2τ)−2τ]^(−2/3); integration constants are fixed by endpoint conditions.

Uses the imported one-dimensional effective-action/superpotential formulation and Borokhov–Gubser auxiliary variables ζi. These turn the linearized second-order equations into a first-order system without requiring the nonsupersymmetric solution to obey the supersymmetric first-order flow.

Rewrite the brick-wall free energy as βF=−Tr e^(−βE), restricting the trace to positive energy and angular momentum, then propose its q-deformed analog. Replace integration over a spacelike hypersurface by a quantum-plane orbit count contributing N².

Construct left-right tensor products of finite cyclic quantum-group modules, specify their generator actions and cyclic closure, and test unitarity through generator-norm inequalities under a changed *-structure.

For matter-free dS3 gravity, the reviewed reduction proceeds from SL(2,C) Chern–Simons theory through a boundary WZNW model to Liouville theory. Asymptotically past-dS boundary conditions supply Hamiltonian-reduction constraints; the classical central charge is c=3ℓ/(2G).

Dimensional reduction on a compact Einstein internal manifold introduces a dynamical radion ψ with potential V(ψ)=(b²/2)e^(−3nψ)−σn(n−1)e^(−(n+2)ψ). Reviewed FLRW solutions accelerate near a radion turning point.

Reviews a spinor construction establishing nonnegative conformal energy for asymptotically dS spacetimes, using a globally timelike conformal Killing vector and the supercovariant derivative ∇̂_μ=∇_μ+iγ_μ/(2ℓ). The detailed presentation specializes to D=4.

For the restricted SU(2) example, selfdual and anti-selfdual base two-forms reduce the BPS system to first-order equations. Cauchy–Riemann relations organize the warp factors into a holomorphic function; the form-field equation discussion also uses harmonicity of B.

The authors decompose ten-dimensional Killing-spinor equations into external and internal equations, impose N=1 spinor projectors, and separate coefficients of the external Weyl spinor and its conjugate.

Spinor bilinears, SU(3) representation decompositions of fluxes and five intrinsic torsion classes relate supersymmetry constraints to internal geometry. Bianchi identities and form-field equations of motion are additionally imposed; supersymmetry variations alone are insufficient.

Determine fermion and 37 couplings using supersymmetric special backgrounds and geometric-symmetry covariance; compare the local results with auxiliary-field calculations in four-dimensional N=1 effective supergravity.

Expand the Einstein-frame Myers DBI plus Chern–Simons action around the wrapped cycle in its normal coordinate, then reduce the eight-dimensional action to light four-dimensional modes, extracting scalar masses, trilinears and fermion masses.

The review uses the N=1 supergravity F-term potential constructed from K and W. The no-scale starting point K=−3 ln(T+T*) and constant W0 is modified by nonperturbative exponentials and an added uplift contribution to study minima and inflationary saddles.

For a long-distance brane potential V(r)=A+B/r^k, the review estimates η using the transverse-volume contribution to Mp. Assuming string-scale coefficients, its dependence on (R/r)^(k+2), together with r≤R, obstructs generic slow roll in a compact space.
Slow-roll parameters and CMB amplitude estimates connect potential flatness to observations. The quoted normalization is δ²=V/(150π²Mp⁴ε), with ε=(MpV′/V)²/2 and historical amplitude δ≈2×10⁻⁵.

Express gravity as BF theory plus quadratic simplicity constraints and matter couplings. The constraints introduce local degrees of freedom; canonical analysis yields Gauss, spatial-diffeomorphism and Hamiltonian constraints.

Construct spin foams as labeled histories of local spin-network moves. History amplitudes multiply vertex factors with a label-dependent normalization; physical amplitudes formally sum over histories. Horizon boundaries use Chern-Simons theory.
Represent the holonomy-flux algebra rather than pointwise canonical fields; construct spin-network states, the Ashtekar-Lewandowski measure, and gauge/spatial-diffeomorphism invariant state spaces.

Use mirror symmetry and special geometry for the worldsheet-instanton-corrected N=2 Kähler potential, followed by a naive N=1 reduction. The quintic/mirror conifold example supplies qualitative motivation for a degenerating Kähler-moduli metric, rather than a complete N=1 calculation.

Analyze the four-dimensional F-term scalar potential using the leading BBHL α′³ correction to K and leading nonperturbative terms in W; study supersymmetry conditions and vary |W0| using continuity arguments for extrema.

Review of intrinsic boundary counterterms generated through the Einstein equations in Gauss–Codazzi form. Variation with respect to the boundary metric gives a stress tensor and Killing charges without embedding into a reference spacetime.
A semiclassical path integral between timelike histories motivates ln Z′=Icl and the Gibbs–Duhem entropy S=βM−Icl. This is the entropy prescription used to test the bounds.

The R-approach evaluates real Lorentzian parameters with imposed periodicity. The C-approach continues t→iT and n→iN. The review states that their results are equivalent under consistent analytic continuation, rather than treating them as independent evidence.

Use a homogeneous radial probe DBI action with Chern-Simons and stabilization potentials. Its early-time solution is r = −R²/t + 9R²/(2H²t³) + …, whose leading term follows the radial light trajectory.

Estimate perturbations from de Sitter scalar fluctuations translated into brane displacement, δr_B = H/(2π√T₃), and a spatially varying inflation-ending delay δt. The paper argues that Lorentz contraction and the moving observer's Hubble enhancement cancel in δr_B.

Independently extract the gravitino mass from the internal part of the ten-dimensional kinetic term and the H-dependent fermion term, with canonical gravitino normalization. Contracting torsion with Ω selects its SU(3)-singlet W1 component.

Reduce the bosonic action using Calabi-Yau-like collective modes, dualize the four-dimensional two-form, and match kinetic terms and the scalar potential to N=1 supergravity. The calculation imports an integrated-curvature formula and uses special Kähler geometry with cubic prepotentials.

Analytically continue smooth, sphere-topology Euclidean Coleman–de Luccia solutions to Lorentzian signature and extend across their horizons. Hartle–Hawking continuation selects asymptotic states; continuation of Euclidean Green functions followed by LSZ is proposed for perturbative scattering.

Use Israel junction conditions to reduce spherical thin-wall motion to a one-dimensional barrier problem. Infer resonance poles from tunneling histories and Fourier transformation of semiclassical actions; Appendix C uses regulated actions in a vanishing-tension limit.

Numerical investigations compare field trajectories and energy fractions with the analytic epoch picture, exhibit bound and unbound solutions, and identify intervals of initial field positions permitting capture.

Approximate analytic solutions divide evolution into four successive epochs: potential domination, kinetic domination, radiation domination, and renewed potential domination. Field values and velocities at each transition supply the next epoch's initial data.

Construct reduction ansätze and substitute them into field equations and supersymmetry variations. Cancellation of internal-coordinate dependence implements consistency of the retained finite field sector. Chapter 4 uses equations rather than actions because some employed symmetries scale the Lagrangian.

Use Iwasawa decomposition and M=LL^T to express scalar kinetic terms covariantly. For group-manifold reductions, Maurer–Cartan forms encode constant structure constants; truncation to left-invariant singlets supplies the consistency argument.

Obtain supersymmetric backgrounds from Killing spinor equations and compatible projection operators. In the supplied 9D particle–string–wall construction, supersymmetry leaves a radial function undetermined; at least one bosonic field equation is additionally used to fix its harmonic form.

Relate de Sitter axion fluctuations to inflationary tensor power, propagate axion entropy perturbations using a large-angle Sachs–Wolfe approximation, and evaluate Gaussian-field moments to obtain isocurvature power and temperature skewness.

Estimate condensate formation from 3H ≃ ma(T), evolve its number density using entropy conservation or the conserved axion-to-decaying-particle number ratio, and implement reheating in the sudden-decay approximation.

Appendix B uses the dilute instanton gas with two-loop running to parameterize the finite-temperature axion mass; Appendix A compares kinetic terms to determine the canonically normalized model-independent string-axion scale.

Reduce democratic type IIB supergravity together with Abelian DBI and Chern–Simons actions. Keep RR fields and their duals until brane couplings are included, then eliminate redundant tensors and magnetic vectors through a Lagrange-multiplier dualization with sources.

Use harmonic Kaluza–Klein expansions, a normal-coordinate expansion of pullbacks, a determinant expansion, and the BPS calibration condition to obtain the Einstein-frame action through second order in derivatives. Identify chiral coordinates by matching its scalar metric to N=1 supergravity.

Differentiate spinorial relations from the superspace torsion and curvature Bianchi identities, then take the spinor trace and two-index/four-index sigma projections to extract the dilaton equation, a divergence equation for L, and its antisymmetrized derivative identity.

Construct component actions and organize connection-dependent variations into f(E), a combination vanishing on the zeroth-order superspace equations. Compare actions through shifts of the torsionful connection and the first-order Taylor expansion underlying removal of equation-of-motion-proportional terms by field redefinitions.

Identify matrix-model discrete transformations and match their actions on momenta, membrane charges and supergraviton helicities to spacetime symmetries; the T3 correspondence additionally uses electric and magnetic fluxes.

Determine twisted-state charges through fermion bosonization and two treatments of bosonic twist operators: OPE branch cuts and explicit rebosonization. The authors report agreement between these charge determinations.

Construct twisted-sector projectors through modular S and T transformations, extract massless spectra, and compute discrete phases of low-energy ’t Hooft operators using instanton zero-mode counts. Perturbative anomaly cancellation supplies a spectrum consistency check.

Monte Carlo sampling of integer fluxes with numerical root finding near the Landau–Ginzburg point. Near the conifold, solve truncated equations for τ and the tangential coordinate ξ, then determine ln Z. Compare weighted counts with rescaled integrals of the index density.

Use imported Picard–Fuchs period solutions and analytic continuation, transform six independent periods to a symplectic basis, and calculate the metric, curvature and Ashok–Douglas density; symbolic algebra is used for curvature expressions.

Probe sensitivity to unknown higher-order Kähler terms by adding δK=d(U+Ū)⁴/(T+T̄)⁴ and comparing potentials through successive orders in ε=u/t. Accept minima only if they persist for a reasonable range of d.

Analyze V=eᴷ(KᴵJ̄FI F̄J̄-3|W|²), FI=WI+KIW. Solve F-equations for supersymmetric extrema and examine the scalar Hessian to distinguish minima from other extrema; use numerical potential searches for additional minima.

Begin with universal one- and two-field toy models, embed their solutions into models with all fields, and use the implicit function theorem to argue persistence under sufficiently small parameter changes when the relevant derivative matrix is nonsingular.

Use the imported generalized supersymmetric attractor equations in rescaled variables: Yᴵ-Ȳᴵ=ipᴵ and FI(Y,Υ)-F̄I(Ȳ,Ῡ)=iqI, with Υ=-64. Solve them on the D=0 charge locus using Yᴬ=wᴬ+ipᴬ/2, where wᴬ is real.

Read the near-horizon radius and area from the corrected central charge, and use the imported Wald entropy formula S=π[|Z|²-256 Im FΥ]. This separates the change in horizon area from the explicit higher-curvature entropy contribution.
Match three- and four-point amplitude coefficients under generalized KLT relations, using selected polarization structures and gauge symmetry; solve the resulting algebraic constraints with Maple.

Background-field one-loop diagrams provide nonanalytic energy-momentum form factors and graviton vacuum polarization. Perturbative Einstein equations and spatial Fourier transforms then produce source metrics.
Use index-line diagrams to count closed tensor traces and identify algebraically leading powers of D. Analyze dimensional dependence from loop integrations separately.

Cubic bosonic OSFT uses a ghost-number-one string field, BRST operator, BPZ product and associative star product. Level (M,N) truncation retains fields through level M and interactions with summed level ≤N; shifted BRST cohomology describes perturbative states around a classical solution.

Other approaches include BSFT's covariant relation ∂iS∝βjGij and noncommutative solitons built from star-product projectors. At large spatial B12, explicit derivatives in the noncommutative plane are suppressed; rank-n projectors represent n codimension-two branes, conditional on the vacuum-energy conjecture.

BCFT constructions use compactification, exactly marginal boundary deformations, bosonization and Wilson lines, followed by decompactification. Boundary-state disk one-point functions determine closed-string sources; Wick rotation produces rolling solutions.

The illustrative disk calculation uses fermion density correlators, WKB asymptotics near the Fermi surface, LSZ reduction for scattering states and a Laplace transform for macroscopic loops. Bosonization identifies asymptotic density waves with tachyon modes.

Boundary Liouville bootstrap uses degenerate operators, conformal Ward identities, hypergeometric conformal blocks and two shift relations. Resonant free-field integrals fix special OPE coefficients and normalization; FZZT/ZZ boundary-state overlaps supply annulus probes.

Matrix fatgraphs generate discretized worldsheets, with powers N^(2−2h) organizing topology. Diagonalization introduces the Vandermonde determinant; a critical double-scaling limit isolates the quadratic maximum of the eigenvalue potential.

A shooting analysis scans the initial field φ₀. After modifying remote potential growth, zeros of h(φ₀)=ρ³φ̇ at the second pole identify regular bounces. The authors track roots that appear or disappear in pairs, at the barrier top or at double zeros.

Small deviations from Hawking-Moss are expanded in Gegenbauer functions C_N^(3/2)(cos y). Cubic and quartic nonlinearities generate coupled mode equations and perturbative amplitude conditions near the linear eigenvalues.

Beyond small amplitudes, the paper combines numerical quartic and sextic examples with analytic matching for a piecewise-linear potential having a flat plateau. The latter uses χ=sin³y dφ/dy to integrate each region.

Trace over the invisible wedge, compare vacuum and excited reduced density matrices, and Taylor-expand von Neumann entropy about the thermal state. The bosonic example uses Minkowski–Rindler Bogoliubov transformations.
Reported Mathematica calculations truncate the occupation-number sum at total occupation N=250. The author studies truncation stability and entropy errors for ω/T=2 and 4, with n up to 1000.
Thermal macrostate counting gives weight exp(−βF), with F=E−TS; black-hole first-law bookkeeping relates absorption energetics to possible entropy loss.

Dimensional reduction of B-brane holomorphic Chern–Simons theory gives holomorphic matrix integrals with action W(Φ)/gs. Their planar eigenvalue distribution computes genus-zero open amplitudes and encodes the transitioned geometry.

GLSM mirror constructions T-dualize chiral-field phases. An instanton-generated exponential superpotential and charge constraints produce a mirror Landau–Ginzburg description, converting A-model instanton questions into B-model period computations.

Open/closed geometric transitions relate conifold Chern–Simons theory to closed strings with t=Ngs. The topological vertex glues Young-diagram-labelled trivalent vertices; torus-invariant ideals and three-dimensional partitions provide a quantum-foam formulation.

Confusion noise is estimated through a redshift integral of n(f,z)h²(f,z), retaining only overlapping events through Θ[n−1]. A z∼1 approximation and a separate network energy-budget estimate give analytic low-frequency background scalings.

Analytic scaling estimates combine loop production per Hubble volume and time, gravitational-radiation lifetimes, and cosmological dilution of surviving older loops to estimate instantaneous loop populations.

Earlier cusp-burst formulas are extended by correcting the loop density, equivalently replacing c by cε/p for ε≲1. Interpolating functions cover nearby, matter-era, and radiation-era emission; a step function excludes Fourier modes below the loop fundamental.

Decompose tensor products of antipodal Fock states into de Sitter representations, extract singlets, reinterpret their coefficients as S-matrix amplitudes, and impose unitarity on those coefficients. Observer bases are organized using rotation Casimirs and Clebsch–Gordan coefficients.

Construct finite conformal representations using spinor-valued symmetric monomials through degree Δ−1/2 together with their inversion duals. Half-integer Δ bounds the representation; fermionic occupation then makes its Fock space finite.

A nonconstant membrane charge gives a nonconserved current. Gauge invariance is maintained by coupling C to its transverse projection; an underlying local construction introduces a Stückelberg two-form and an auxiliary constraint before integrating them out.

Solving the four-form equation and incorporating membrane-induced flux jumps produces effective scalar vacuum equations labelled by an integer n. Near the attractor, the approximate relation F0=nqeff(φ) makes the scanning step field-dependent.

Vacua are counted by accumulating elementary changes until the scalar VEV changes by order itself. Membrane-localized mass effects are studied using energy estimates and localized tachyonic modes; axionic domain walls provide a resolved membrane realization.

Gauge transformations and covariant derivatives are computed directly. Comparing their variations with the required transformation of Da gives an antisymmetric charge constraint, also obtained by evaluating commutators of embedded gauge generators.

Nonabelian embeddings are analyzed through structure constants and Lie-algebra cohomology. On the compactification side, deformed differential relations among internal forms and the NS Bianchi identity reproduce the same charge constraints.

RR scalars and charges are organized into symplectic vectors, with a symmetric symplectic matrix M governing their kinetic term. Minimal coupling then constructs the gauged sigma-model kinetic terms and its vector-boson mass matrix.

Partition-function phases use real K-theory and a mod-2 Dirac index. The untwisted anomaly argument uses an AHSS-compatible polarization, a degree-five characteristic, Poincaré duality, and liftability of degree-two integral classes to K-theory.

The no-go argument loops a classifying-space fibration, classifies homotopy-associative H-space actions and extensions using integral power series and a cobar calculation, then constrains the first Postnikov invariant.
The cobordism argument uses the stable-range map Σ∞K(Z,6) → Σ⁶HZ, asserted to be a 12-equivalence, then connective spin bordism and the Thom isomorphism to reduce the calculation to H5(BSpin,Z)=0.

The authors compare the AdS depth, gravitino mass and uplifted barrier, then examine loss of stabilization under additional inflationary energy. For the racetrack extension they impose W=DρW=0 to locate a supersymmetric Minkowski extremum and distinguish it from supersymmetric AdS extrema with W≠0.

They report calculations and potential plots using SuperCosmology. The plotted complex-modulus potential is offered as support for locating the proposed example's minimum at α=0; this record does not independently reproduce those calculations.

For gauged solutions the authors use an ansatz inspired by Kerr–Newman–AdS and the ungauged pairwise-equal solution, followed by direct substitution into the equations of motion using Mathematica. They report analogous equation checks for the gauged NUT extension.

Reduce along time, dualise three-dimensional vectors to axions, apply four O(1,1) charge-generating transformations, then explicitly undualise and lift. Computationally, transform M=VᵀηV through M′=ΛᵀMΛ, avoiding the compensating transformation needed to restore Borel gauge.

For the symmetric torus, eliminate variables to obtain a cubic for Re τ and algebraic equations for Im τ, yielding extension degree at most six for the analyzed isolated solutions. Exact algebraic solutions also support Monte Carlo enumeration; hypersurface calculations use local period expansions.

At fixed moduli, expand periods and their relevant derivatives in a finite extension F/Q. Equations become integer linear constraints: generically η=D(h2,1+1) constraints on 2b3 flux integers, with D additional constraints for W=0. Dimension-based L estimates require independence and positive remaining dimension.

Use heights of primitive rational coordinates and polynomial coefficients to estimate lattice-solution densities and sum over allowed moduli. These are order-of-magnitude arguments; correlated coefficients, separately vanishing terms and logarithmic enhancements can invalidate naive formulas.

Five-brane dynamics is approximated by a single-field effective potential, studied graphically and through a small-position quadratic expansion. Canonical normalization, slow-roll parameters and approximate Friedmann evolution give illustrative inflation and fluctuation estimates.

The author uses a four-dimensional supergravity Kähler potential with flux, hidden-sector gaugino-condensate and open-membrane superpotentials; supersymmetric stabilization is analyzed through Kähler-covariant equations D_i W = 0.

Solve vanishing moduli F-terms for supersymmetric stationary points and classify local minima through real-modulus and axion Hessian blocks and their determinants. Add the power-law uplift of eq. (8), with nonnegative integer exponents nt,ns, tuning D to zero or small positive vacuum energy.

Compute soft terms using visible-sector superspace couplings, combining tree-level moduli mediation with anomaly mediation and mixed contributions. Retained orders include one-loop gaugino/A terms and mixed scalar terms, and two-loop pure anomaly scalar masses.

Connects the A model through an auxiliary two-form action, semiclassical elimination and BRST gauge fixing. Tests the proposed B-model Wigner-function relation through a tree-level steepest-descent calculation.
Uses Hitchin's Hamiltonian flow: ∂tρ = dk and ∂tσ = −dρ̂, with Hamiltonian H = 2VS(σ) − VH(ρ), to relate six-dimensional SU(3) data to seven-dimensional G2 geometry.

Uses homogeneous volume functionals of stable forms, reconstructs geometric structures algebraically, and varies closed forms within fixed de Rham cohomology classes. These are Hitchin constructions imported as the mathematical basis.

Use high-temperature Yang–Mills free energy through order g^2, generated by one- and two-loop diagrams. Its negative expansion coefficient α2 makes free energy increase with coupling. With g^2 = κ/Φ, the thermal potential contains +T^4 a2/Φ, with a2 > 0.

Locate the critical temperature by simultaneous vanishing of the first and second modulus derivatives of Veff. Approximating the slowly varying thermal contribution as linear gives V''(Φcrit) = 0 and Tcrit = [-V'(Φcrit)/vth'(Φcrit)]^(1/4), relating destabilization to the maximal zero-temperature slope.
Regulate the noncompact Killing-horizon area at r=R and integrate the bulk Einstein action radially to extract the induced four-dimensional Newton constant: 1/G4=(1/(lG5))∫[ri,R] r dr.

Construct bulk α-vacua by Bogoliubov transformation of Euclidean modes. Obtain the black-hole Euclidean Wightman function through an image sum of the AdS propagator, then use antipodal terms to construct Gα.
Probe the states using scalar-coupled particle detectors, a modified point-splitting stress-tensor prescription, and analytic continuation through a Euclidean section to Kruskal coordinates.

Construct orbifold actions and gauge-shift embeddings subject to modular invariance, supplemented by quantized Wilson lines. Compare one-loop differential-running coefficients above and below the compactification scale.

Compare the lowest heterotic excitation with dual type I string or heterotic M-theory KK thresholds; use S/T duality networks to estimate dangerous light states. Separately estimate the 10d gauge-theory one-loop/tree ratio using a cutoff Λ=m_H and group factors.

Wilsonian matching is organized into three stages: integrate out brane fields, solve the classical bulk response to their effective sources, and then integrate quantum bulk fluctuations. The desired four-dimensional vacuum energy is the result below 1/r.

Heavy bulk modes are treated through local six-dimensional bulk and brane operators constrained by covariance and locality. Their contributions are combined with light-mode Casimir energies to obtain the radion potential, rather than using an unconstrained sum of four-dimensional KK vacuum energies.

Timelike solutions are encoded by a complex function F and real conformal factor φ depending on x, y, z, together with a determined shift one-form. Writing F = A + iB gives A = ∂zφ and two coupled nonlinear equations for B and φ, obtainable from a reduced action.

Special reductions use a Liouville equation for magnetic solutions with A = A(z), dimensionally reduced gravitational Chern-Simons solutions for kink configurations, and harmonic F with holomorphic coefficient functions for further wave families. These are explicit construction methods for restricted timelike sectors.

Construct differential forms from a Killing spinor, use Fierz identities for algebraic constraints, and impose their differential constraints plus Maxwell equations and Bianchi identity. Einstein equations then follow in the timelike case; the null case additionally requires the Einstein component along V ⊗ V.

Tracks the Hubble rate at each mode's creation rather than substituting only its current value into the energy density. Differentiation with respect to the scale factor determines q; the resulting differential equation is solved for H(a).
Uses the imported horizon-thermodynamic framework: S=πMp²/H², T=H/(2π), and dQ=T dS motivate retaining Ḣ=−4π(ρ+p)/Mp² when introducing sources.

Compares the approximations against author-performed brute-force enumeration of the allowed eight- and six-dimensional configurations. These comparisons support qualitative distributions and, for some normalized observables, reasonably close numerical agreement.

Generalizes integer-partition generating functions to tadpole counting. Contour integrals impose integer constraints; summing stack multiplicities produces geometric series. Numerical saddle points and Hessian corrections give multivariable semi-analytic estimates.
Uses factorization identities, gcd conditions implementing coprime wrapping numbers, and supersymmetry/tadpole bounds to restrict admissible branes and complex-structure ratios.

Counts critical points using an ensemble integral with δ(V′)|det V″|, imposing Hessian positivity for metastability. The determinant is the Jacobian giving unit weight per isolated vacuum, physically involving the product of bosonic squared masses.

Rewrites stationarity as an eigenvector problem for a Hermitian block matrix built from the complex symmetric Z=D²W. Uses unitary factorization of Z, the paired spectrum, eigenvalue-measure Jacobians, and small-F expansions of the bosonic mass matrix.

Uses the imported boundary-EFT derivative expansion and mixed condition ∂nφ=−κφ. Translates κ into Bogoliubov coefficients, uses Klein–Gordon-normalized de Sitter modes, and expands the initial-state Green function through second order.

Computes one-loop stress-tensor expectations from differentiated equal-time Green functions. Smooth cutoff integrals separate oscillatory and nonoscillatory contributions; bulk composite-operator renormalization and boundary counterterms receive separate prescriptions.

Uses explicit time-dependent S-brane solutions and Einstein-frame dimensional reduction. Canonical scalar redefinitions expose exponential potentials; a time reparametrization and autonomous-variable analysis classify single-scalar trajectories and fixed points.

For quartic corrections, substitutes constant external/internal expansion rates to obtain algebraic equations solved numerically. Linear exponential perturbations classify five stability modes. The appendix distinguishes the lapse constraint from the two dynamical equations.
Reviews the warped Einstein-equation no-go argument: positivity of a stress-tensor combination and integration by parts constrain the warp factor, provided surface terms vanish.

Compute one-form flux energy ∫Σ F∧*F by changing from an integral cycle basis to holomorphic forms and applying the Hodge star. The period-matrix treatment is explicit for h=1,2,3; higher-form flux energies contract corresponding matrices from each surface.

Balance positive, negative, positive terms at successive perturbative orders, schematically ag²−bg³+cg⁴. Analyze relative volumes using symmetry and the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, then stabilize an overall volume–coupling combination before treating subdominant terms.
Solve the N=4 auxiliary-field and Poincaré gauge-fixing constraints after the Z2×Z2 truncation, then separate the holomorphic superpotential from the gravitino mass using m3/2=e^(K/2)W.

Identify flux-induced superpotential structures by comparing dimensionally reduced scalar potentials in the IIA field basis. Combine them through antisymmetric gauging structure constants satisfying Jacobi identities; the off-diagonal S/A basis simplifies the plane-symmetric cyclicity equations.

Dimensional reduction of the ten-dimensional action, elimination of the spacetime three-form and dualization of the two-form determine the scalar potential and charged axion covariant derivatives. The authors compare the result with the general electric N=2 gauged-supergravity potential.

Mirror symmetry supplies instanton-corrected vector-multiplet data through periods, Picard–Fuchs solutions and symplectic transformations. The sextic example uses periods expanded through sixth order near the Landau–Ginzburg point; known universal-hypermultiplet loop corrections are then incorporated.

Dualize the nondynamical four-dimensional three-form including its Chern–Simons couplings. This supplies a real integration constant and terms involving G∧a3 and da3∧a3 that a purely linear flux coupling would miss.
Reduce gravitino bilinears after Einstein-frame rescaling, separating internal-spinor derivative, internal-flux and external-three-form contributions. Match the resulting gravitino mass to e^(K/2)W.

Linearize the weak-G2 equations with the varied Hodge star, decompose three-forms into G2 representations, and use Q=*d and Laplace eigenforms. Compare the reduced bosonic potential with the standard N=1 F-term expression.

Use the D9 κ-symmetry projector together with covariantly constant spinors to obtain magnetic holomorphy F_(2,0)=0 and a nonlinear DBI calibration condition. Holomorphy constrains τ; the calibration equation constrains Kähler parameters.

Solve polynomial flux constraints on τ and, after eliminating off-diagonal Kähler components, a linear system for the products J2J3, J1J3 and J1J2. Impose separately total D9 R-R charge 16, vanishing induced D5 charge on every two-cycle, and positive calibrated volumes.
Apply a cited two-throat tunneling amplitude, compare estimated tunneling and decay times, and use the standard reheating-temperature estimate with a transferred energy fraction P.

Estimate interaction strengths by dimensional reduction and warp-factor counting in Einstein–Hilbert overlap integrals and brane couplings. The appendix gives a complementary four-dimensional supergravity analysis using canonical brane fields.
Use static AdS spin-two KK wavefunctions expressed through Bessel functions, normalize them with the warped measure and retain their leading exponential behavior toward the throat tips.

Qualitative gravitational effective-field-theory arguments combine false-vacuum bubble construction, black-hole formation, and analytic continuation of CDL instantons. These are applications of imported semiclassical results.

AdS/CFT arguments compare black-hole and CFT entropy, interpret domain-wall equations through holographic renormalization-group flow, and compare candidate CFT operator spectra with large-radius Kaluza–Klein expectations.

Use axion/form duality to determine the Euclidean continuation and the additional surface term defining the instanton action. The universal hypermultiplet continuation is motivated through its double-tensor formulation.

Solve the Euclidean field equations using the radial ansatz ds²=e^{2B(r)}(dr²+r²dΩ²), with radial scalar fields. The general solution is expressed through a harmonic function on the conformally flat geometry; the negative-invariant branch is rewritten using trigonometric functions.

Reduce the six-dimensional Einstein and form equations directly, impose three-form self-duality, and identify a four-dimensional Lagrangian reproducing the resulting equations. Reduce the gravitino variation separately.

Use real spinor bilinears and their algebraic/differential identities to obtain a Killing vector K, a closed one-form L, adapted coordinates K=∂t and L=dy, and a conformally flat two-dimensional transverse metric. Integrability commutators identify the remaining equations of motion.

Uses conformal-gauge Nambu-string solutions as sums of left- and right-movers to explain cusp formation. Observational reasoning combines lensing, CMB effects, pulsar timing, cusp/kink bursts and population statistics.

Reviews causal Kibble production, reconnection and loop formation, simulation-based network scaling, and decay through gravitational radiation. Stability is analyzed through topology, domain-wall confinement and Schwinger-suppressed endpoint pair creation.
Test geometric conditions using T2 fibrations over K3 with integral curvature classes and K3 lattice periods, and a one-parameter SU(3)-structure family on the Iwasawa manifold.

Decompose fluxes and supersymmetry equations into irreducible SU(3) representations. Spinor contractions with gamma matrices extract equivalent tensor conditions; exterior derivatives of spinor bilinears determine intrinsic torsion.
Use integrability of the gravitino and dilatino equations, together with form Bianchi identities and equations of motion, to reduce the independent field-equation checks.

Perform harmonic Kaluza–Klein reduction with orientifold constraints, equivalently truncate the N=2 action, then Weyl-rescale and identify the standard N=1 couplings. Dualizing the four-dimensional three-form introduces the constant electric flux e0.
