Use special-geometry period identities and a Legendre transform between linear and chiral multiplets to treat a general parity-adapted symplectic basis. A Lagrangian embedding gives an alternative geometric interpretation of the reduced quaternionic sector.

Use the Einstein action with boundary extrinsic-curvature terms and intrinsic counterterms cancelling divergences. Vary the boundary metric to obtain a stress tensor and construct charges from boundary Killing vectors. Adopt the Gibbs–Duhem entropy S=lim(βH Qχ−I), where Qχ is the charge associated with the horizon generator.

Adopt c=(Gμν nμ nν)⁻¹ with n the unit vector in the τ direction, and define its area average over the angular two-surface at fixed t and τ. Compare its asymptotic behavior with the expanding-patch dS c-theorem.

Identify determinant observables with brane partition functions and Baker–Akhiezer functions. The charged functions belong to the Zakharov–Shabat hierarchy, while the neutral function obeys the 0A hierarchy's operator equations.

Analyze asymptotic solutions, Stokes sectors and WKB eigenvalue curves, then interpret disk and annulus terms through super-Liouville boundary states and RR vertex insertions. A neutral determinant inserted at x=0 implements a unit change in |q|.

Use a modified Painlevé II bulk string equation and a compatible flat linear system for charged branes. Schlesinger/Bäcklund transformations relate neighboring integer-flux sectors and propagate physical boundary conditions from q=0.

Use monopole quantization, root/coroot lattices and the centralizer of the magnetic weight. The remaining electric source is a representation of the magnetic stabilizer; Weyl stabilizers repackage this information as a simultaneous orbit of two weights.

Boundary variations of the action and Wilson insertion determine the electric background, including the θ-dependent shift. Classical stress tensors evaluated on the prescribed backgrounds give Gaussian results or leading weak-coupling terms.

A Weyl rescaling by r^−2 maps the complement of the line to H²×S². Line insertions become boundary conditions preserving all isometries, making the symmetry restriction on admissible singularities explicit.

The massless scalar radial equation is transformed into a Schrödinger problem. A near-throat potential proportional to λ²sinh²z is analyzed with WKB quantization and elliptic-integral asymptotics; the available exact Toda-lattice technique is not used.
The asymptotic expansion of the deformed metric is inserted into a holographic boundary stress-tensor formula to calculate its trace and investigate a possible boundary mass scale.

Linear-response theory relates relaxation to thermal two-point functions and their frequency-space poles. Euclidean torus correlators are analytically continued to real time; semiclassical contributions are organized by modular images of the boundary torus.

Generalize earlier bundle-extension constructions to build Z3×Z3-equivariant SU(4) bundles on X̃ and descend them to X. The multiplet-splitting method is explicitly credited to earlier work rather than introduced as wholly new here.
Constrain hidden-sector bundles through [W]=c2(TX̃)−c2(Ṽ)−c2(Ṽ′). Effectivity of this class permits a wrapped holomorphic five-brane in strong coupling; weak coupling requires [W]=0.

Compute massless zero modes from bundle cohomology and the Atiyah–Singer index. For each Spin(10) representation, tensor the group action on its cohomology with the Wilson-line action, then retain the joint Z3×Z3-invariant subspace.

Lorentz spinor harmonics isolate the irreducible κ-invariant fermion and convert target-space spinor equations into worldvolume Dirac equations. This is presented as an alternative to imposing static gauge and explicitly breaking the target Lorentz group.

Expand known superembedding or covariant-action fermionic equations to first order in fermions, then read off the quadratic action. The linear supervielbein expansion supplies the spin connection and flux-dependent superspace torsion.

Large-N vacuum counting approximates additive observables by Gaussian distributions using central-limit arguments and Fourier representations of the vacuum density. The paper distinguishes a dense central distribution from rare tails and exponentially fine vacuum spacings.

Phenomenological constructions use renormalization-group running, dimensional transmutation, thermal dark-matter freezeout and environmental bounds. Negative-quartic metastability is discussed using Euclidean bounce methods and a running quartic coupling.

Compute the four-dimensional F-term potential from the supplied Kähler potential and open-membrane superpotential. Retain the brane–brane contribution W₅₅ and impose D_αW₅₅=D_iW₅₅=0 as conditions for partial minimization.

Approximate the brane-position metric by 2δ_ij/(Qt), retain nearest-neighbor interactions, and use equal complex separations. Separate the center-of-mass field and rescale the common difference field to obtain a single canonically normalized exponential potential.

Support for the dynamics comes from low-energy open-string scattering/cylinder interaction potentials and tachyonic modes. T-duality along shared directions relates a p−1 dimensional Dp intersection to intersecting D-strings.
Generic intersection dimensions are obtained by geometrical dimension counting. Toroidal winding and successive reconnections then provide the proposed route from intersection to disappearance.
Adapt the Garriga–Mukhanov perturbation formalism: solve v″−c_s²∇²v−(z″/z)v=0 with a Bunch–Davies vacuum and match across sound-horizon crossing c_sk=aH.

Use the Einstein-coupled probe DBI and Chern–Simons action, homogeneous FRW equations, a near-light-speed asymptotic expansion, and comparisons of probe versus source energy to estimate backreaction limits.
Geometric transitions construct the alternate metric; T-dual brane boxes interpret wrapped-D3 states. Weierstrass/Tate equations and discriminants organize exceptional symmetry configurations.
Componentwise Einstein and G-flux equations, including selected curvature corrections and moving membrane sources, are combined with an integrated warp-factor/anomaly equation.

Expand φ=φ₀+φ̃ and apply φ̄=Ω^((2−D)/4)φ̃. Match the position-dependent quadratic term through m²Ω=M²(x), and use the conformal kinetic-term identity to obtain a curvature coupling and transformed interactions.

Use an SO(D)-invariant radial ansatz for the nonlinear Laplace equation, then promote the profile's position and size parameters to moduli. Compute their Hitchin information metric by integrating L₀ ∂I(log L₀) ∂J(log L₀), with a chosen normalization.

World-sheet conformal field theory, bosonic twist fields and the stress-energy method determine disk three- and four-point amplitudes. For factorizable toroidal cycles, calculations separate into contributions from the three two-tori.

Dimensional reduction of world-volume actions supplies holomorphic gauge kinetic functions. Reviewed stabilization methods use the Type IIB flux superpotential W = integral of Ω3 wedge G3 and leading-instanton nonperturbative superpotentials from confining gauge sectors.

Homology and oriented intersection numbers determine net chiral spectra. R-R tadpoles are obtained from supergravity and D-brane source couplings; symplectic probe branes diagnose additional discrete K-theory constraints.

For energy conditions, the authors contract proposed stress tensors with future timelike vectors and examine positivity and causal energy flow. Their noncommutative tensors replace the interaction potential by integrals along a path from a reference point to the observation point.

Light-cone momentum integrals separate a kinematic exponential from an interaction kernel. Large-q+ asymptotics and contour rotations establish a vanishing region. Nonplanar transverse integrals are analyzed with θ in canonical two-dimensional blocks to extract the changed exponential behavior.

Canonical interaction-picture quantization and time-ordered evolution expand a Heisenberg-field commutator matrix element through order g². The chosen bra and ket are the same evolved perturbative vacuum; M(1) vanishes for the φ3 interaction.

Compute torus partition functions by enumerating commuting lifts in G of effective-quotient boundary conditions. Check omitted sectors and sector multiplicities against SL(2,Z) orbits; noncentral kernels can produce different multiplicities between orbits.

Represent trivial cyclic twist fields through finite sums over roots of unity. Use conformal perturbation theory and Landau-Ginzburg superpotential deformations to describe twisted-sector expectation values algebraically.

Quantize branches labelled by principal G-bundles on S1; compare the resulting state multiplicities with one-loop pole expansions. Test competing spectrum interpretations through higher-loop factorization and fusion-rule closure.

Apply harmonic analysis and Selberg trace formulas to Dirac heat kernels on odd-dimensional hyperbolic quotients with cusps. The construction uses Iwasawa/Langlands decompositions, half-spin representations, intertwining operators and orbital integrals.

Construct homogeneous vector bundles from K representations and express their connection Laplacians using Casimir operators. For the arithmetic H³ quotient, relate invariant kernels to analytic spectral test functions through the Selberg transform.

Substitute the Freund–Rubin ansatz into the bosonic equations, then impose vanishing gravitino variation. Killing-spinor integrability is expressed through Weyl-tensor contractions, separating Einstein solutions from supersymmetric ones.

Compute tree-level B-twisted Landau-Ginzburg correlators by summing observables divided by the Hessian determinant over critical points and finite-field values. Root-valued fields are BRST invariant, lack superpartners and are omitted from Hessian differentiation.

Expand Higgs fields in holomorphic zero modes to construct GLSM map-moduli stacks. Infer A-model correlators from their dimensions and compare quantum-cohomology relations with those obtained from one-loop effective gauge actions.

Apply Morrison-Plesser-Hori-Vafa dualization, introducing periodic neutral Y fields and gauge multiplets Σ. Integrating out Σ imposes constraints with discrete root-of-unity branches; integrating out Y reproduces effective gauge superpotentials.

Separate the potential into two nonperturbative terms and an α′ term, compute their large-volume scalings, and minimize the relevant axion to obtain negative interference. For the two-modulus example, solve approximate stationary equations and compare with numerical minima.

Begin with the no-scale flux potential, solve DₐW=0 for complex structure and dilaton, and then study Kähler moduli using the leading O(α′³) Kähler correction and nonperturbative superpotential contributions from D3 instantons or D7 gaugino condensation.

Branch the embedding tensor under dimensional-reduction subgroups and assign E7(7) weights from dilaton-dependent quadratic terms. T-duality is represented by sign reversals of the relevant internal weight-basis vectors.

A solvable-Lie-algebra parametrization tracks the eleven-dimensional origin of scalars. The Scherk–Schwarz Killing vector gives ∂_y S(x,y)|_0=k_M(S), which is interpreted as background flux or torsion.

Use generalized gauge transformations δA_M=C_M^N(y)∂_NΛ(x), then compute the torsionful spin connection and reduced couplings through contorsion. Requiring only reduced gauge invariance permits more torsion components than full higher-dimensional gauge invariance.
Boundary stress tensors, extrinsic curvature and AdS counterterms are used to compute masses and finite on-shell actions; asymptotic falloffs encode the charges that tunneling must preserve.
Explicit coordinate scalings and Inönü–Wigner contractions track how the AdS quotient generator becomes either a translation or a boost in inequivalent flat limits.
Euclidean bounce construction requires matching asymptotics and a nonconformal negative mode. Continuing an angle of the bounce's S3 through its equator produces the Lorentzian expanding bubble.

For strong SU(2M) factors with Nf=Nc, introduce mesons and baryons and impose det M−B B̃=Λ^{4M} through a superpotential multiplier. Mesonic vevs Higgs spectator groups; integrating out massive fields exposes the residual quiver and probe geometry.

Construct candidate Seiberg-duality cycles and examine rank changes and gauge-coupling beta functions. Repetition of a quiver alone does not establish that its duality sequence is realizable as an RG cascade.

Use equilibrium sub-web separations to describe complex deformations. A topological flux count restricts fractional-brane assignments: if only k of n asymptotic three-cycles remain nontrivial after deformation, only k independent flux choices survive in a purely geometric completion.

Use the singular-fibration spectral sequence with groups Hᵖ(B,Rᑫπ*Z). Twisting introduces d₂ maps; Poincaré duality and the universal coefficient theorem determine a remaining torsion group when the lower map cannot be computed directly.

Cut out a neighbourhood shaped like a rugby ball around a base path and reglue its torus fibres by twisting one circle, with angular shift Nθ. The twist number N equals the selected integral flux. The author calls this surgery while explicitly distinguishing it from standard surgery.

Invoke imported Wall–Žubr classification and minimal-model/formality results to assess topological information. The classification requires spin and simple connectivity, intersection and Pontrjagin data, with refined invariants when torsion is present.
Analyze covariant F-term equations D_iW = D_SW = D_TW = 0, using D_iΩ = χ_i, Hodge decompositions and quantized flux-period pairings to constrain flux components and moduli.

Compare the dimensional-reduction complete-square potential with the four-dimensional supergravity potential. The discussion identifies the K_iW_GC term and a dilaton covariant-derivative factor as sources of their differing stabilization conditions.

Analytic stationarity conditions and very special geometry identities are used to derive Hessians. Stability is assessed through metric-raised Hessian eigenvalues; symmetry reductions and trace/determinant tests simplify the stable-family calculation.

Mathematica supplies the generic stable family's scalar spectrum and assists searches for extrema in the studied SL(3,C)/SU(3) models. Negative search results should retain this computational provenance.

Quantize first-order BPS attractor-flow equations as supersymmetric Wheeler–DeWitt constraints in a local quantum mechanics with four supercharges. This fixes a semiclassical wave function more strongly than the Hamiltonian constraint alone.

Perform Dirac reduction to the BPS phase space, then geometric quantization. The reported brackets are [X^I,X̄^J]=(2/π)(Imτ)⁻¹ᴵᴶ and, for χ^I=ReX^I and η_I=ReF_I, [χ^I,η_J]=δ^I_J/(πi). Real polarization quantizes H³(M,R).

Exchange the roles of Euclidean spatial and temporal directions and cut the cylinder into two pieces. The authors interpret the resulting trace-versus-state-overlap relation as a target-space analogue of open/closed channel duality.

Use Euclidean Hartle–Hawking path integrals, expand the logarithm of the wavefunctional in boundary fields, and analytically continue to future infinity. Boundary scaling data provide the proposed perturbative gauge-invariant mass diagnostic.

Match thermal probabilities for Poincare-energy eigenspaces to the static-Hamiltonian ensemble; model black-hole entropy deficits using annihilation constraints on blocks of rectangular canonical fermion matrices.

Apply sequential Seiberg dualities with Nc′=Nf−Nc, meson introduction and removal of massive pairs. Identify the confined geometry through mesonic branches, quantum constraints det Mi−Bi B̃i=Λ^(4M), and ADS superpotentials when Nf<Nc.

Use toric and (p,q)-web diagrams: separate equilibrium subwebs to describe complex deformations, or add them to construct a parent geometry with a desired terminal singularity. Obtain the quotient quiver by geometric and Chan–Paton orbifold projection.

Determine generic shift breaking through the rank and kernels of the flux/twist map on gauge parameters. Construct Goldstone fields with an inverse on its nondegenerate block and form massive vector combinations.

Reduce a left-invariant metric and p-form ansatz, including a locally defined flux potential. Derive covariant field strengths, gauge transformations and the scalar potential, and organize the common-sector action using an O(d,d) generalized metric.
Use a restricted integer flux search, then solve DτW=0 numerically with K=K0−2 log V and W=W0+Σ48 bE exp(−2πτE)+Σ12 cD exp(−2πτD/6). The authors subsequently evaluate full DW and a 51×51 mass matrix.

Toric resolutions determine divisor intersections and Mori/Kähler cones. Birational factorizations into blow-ups and contractions transfer exceptional-divisor properties between phases; a relative homology argument addresses third cohomology.

Apply the harmonic projector H to the sourced equation. Once its cohomological obstruction vanishes, use the Green operator G, with 1−H=ΔG, to construct a particular solution and add harmonic homogeneous solutions.
Use Dolbeault Hodge theory to identify fluxless solutions with harmonic forms, and a form-level Serre-duality map to replace normal-bundle-valued forms by ordinary odd-degree forms.
Represent Clifford multiplication by wedge and contraction operators, decomposing the positive worldvolume-chirality spinor into ordinary even forms and K-valued even forms.

Construct a component-dependent dual RR action, treating selected potentials and dual field strengths independently. Potentials act as Lagrange multipliers whose equations produce Bianchi identities; choosing the appropriate dualization places the surviving four-dimensional axions in chiral multiplets.

Solve the Bianchi identities, substitute the field strengths into the action, and perform generalized dimensional reduction. Combine curvature, NSNS, RR and localized-source contributions, using sourced identities to reconstruct the N=1 potential and obtain a geometrical superpotential.

Construct antibrane spurion operators using the chiral compensator and Weyl scaling; solve auxiliary-field equations and minimize the uplifted potential to obtain canonically normalized tree-level soft terms.

Include anomaly mediation through one-loop RG dependence of gauge kinetic functions and matter wavefunctions, retaining anomaly–modulus mixed contributions to scalar masses at energies just below compactification.

Solve the N=4 scalar constraints in variables exposing geometric moduli and the dilaton. Read e^(K/2)W from the projected gravitino mass matrix, separating its non-holomorphic normalization from its holomorphic polynomial.

Determine the IIA complex variables from scalar and D6 gauge kinetic terms, then match flux-induced scalar potentials to the N=1 potential. Combined fluxes are encoded by consistent gauge-algebra structure constants.

Split the pulled-back target-space connection into intrinsic connection, normal-bundle connection and extrinsic curvature. Reexpress the intrinsic derivative in the deformed frame to isolate the canonical Dirac operator.
Use an adapted local frame to factor 1+X into a Lorentz transformation and T=√(1−X²), then deform the vielbein by T and rotate the fermions by exp(RΓ̃(10)).

Reorganize the previously derived additional kinetic terms using gamma-matrix identities and an iterative series in the worldvolume field strength, resumming them into an inverse matrix multiplying the supergravity spinor derivative.

Match dual descriptions through gauged N=2 supergravity and symplectic sections. A symplectic exchange involving ρ and F_ρ identifies the D3-instanton function with ∂_ρ f, where f is the dual world-sheet-instanton prepotential.

Use toric Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces and Gromov–Witten invariants to compute instanton expansions and multicovers. The restricted generalized-GVW derivation additionally uses the c-map, stable degeneration and mirror symmetry.

The F-string action includes the Kalb–Ramond coupling with μ = T. The D-string calculation uses Born–Infeld plus Chern–Simons terms, without a worldsheet gauge field; the latter changes the angular stability condition.

Uses the Nambu–Goto equations and conformal-gauge constraints. In M⁴ × S¹, the known traveling-wave ansatz x = a(σ−t), θ = σ + b(σ−t) satisfies the equations when b(b+1) + |a′|² = 0 and the internal periodicity is respected.

For circular conifold embeddings, fixes X⁰ = t and X¹/X² = tan σ, obtains conserved energy and angular momentum, and studies quadratic fluctuations around τ = 0. Fourier modes of sphere fluctuations are used to assess σ-dependent perturbations.

Kähler transformations and holomorphic field redefinitions expose the shift symmetry. The authors calculate the Kähler metric and F-term scalar potential, canonically normalize the real fields, and analyze extrema of the modulus-dependent mass and offset functions.

Background evolution is obtained by numerical integration of two Klein–Gordon equations and the Friedmann equation using e-fold time N. Tangential slow-roll parameters and a transverse potential-curvature diagnostic characterize the trajectory and its termination.

Compares that expansion with multi-center attractor solutions and their Euclidean continuations. The function S(x), related to local entropy, is used as a Euclidean-time variable to describe branching into separate throats.

Uses the U(N) representation sum and its equivalent system of N free nonrelativistic fermions on a circle. Large-N fluctuations near the two Fermi surfaces give chiral and antichiral amplitudes; finite-depth holes expose overcounting in their product.

Grand-canonical generating functions organize particle/hole corrections. A formal regularization and analytic-continuation prescription yields a quadratic recursion, iterated into a signed Catalan expansion. Inverse transforms then recast charge-sector indices as wavefunction norms.
Numerically evolve two first-order background equations, mainly for Λ=0, with V(T)=V₀/cosh(T/√2). Estimate inflationary e-folds from the area under the plateau of H(t).
Reduce the background equations to Hdot/(H²−λ²)=−3 Tdot²/2. With F(t)=(3/2)∫₀ᵗ Tdot² dt′+H₀⁻¹, integrate to H=1/F for Λ=0 and H=λ coth(λF) for Λ>0; this still requires determining T(t).

Dimensional reduction and volume power counting organize higher-derivative corrections. Moduli masses are extracted from potential derivatives after approximate canonical normalization near the minimum.

The matter expansion of K and W supplies standard supergravity formulas for scalar masses, gaugino masses and trilinears. D3 effective μ terms are generated through a Kähler-potential bilinear using the Giudice–Masiero mechanism.
Uses a Dirac–Born–Infeld-derived brane-gas equation of state and FRW continuity, Friedmann, and acceleration equations. The modulus is evolved with φ̈ + dHφ̇ + V′(φ) = 0.

Analyzes approximate potential-dominated and kinetic-dominated epochs, then numerically solves the acceleration and modulus equations with initial data satisfying the Friedmann constraint. Bound and diluted-gas unbound examples illustrate dependence on source abundance.

Studies deformed superpotential products and spherical harmonics, estimates KK scales from internal-cycle volumes, evaluates Wilson strings and wrapped-D5 probe actions, and takes pp-wave limits to investigate composites of KK modes.

Uses the imported Lunin–Maldacena solution-generating prescription: separate a two-isometry torus, organize IIB fields into SL(3,R) multiplets, transform M=ggᵀ by M→ΛMΛᵀ, and extract transformed metric, dilaton and form fields.

Direct dimensional reduction of massive IIA supergravity gives a zero-mode potential including flux and O6 contributions. Eliminating the nondynamical spacetime-polarized F4 fixes the RR axion combination; extrema and quadratic fluctuation masses are then analyzed.

Using the imported orientifold effective-action framework, the authors solve D_iW=0 with W=∫Ω_c∧H3+e0+e_a t^a+(1/2)κ_abc m^a t^b t^c−(m0/6)κ_abc t^a t^b t^c. Complex-structure and Kähler equations decouple; the dilaton is fixed afterward.

Cancels brane-source poles by choosing ℓᴵⱼ=−Cᴵⱼₖkⱼᴶkⱼᴷ/(2qⱼ) and mⱼ=Cᴵⱼₖkⱼᴵkⱼᴶkⱼᴷ/(12qⱼ²). Solves the curl equation for ω using pairwise vector fields without Dirac–Misner strings, producing constraints on intercenter distances.

Reuses a linear BPS algorithm involving self-dual dipole field strengths and harmonic functions. GH solutions are described by eight harmonic functions V, Kᴵ, Lᴵ and M, with Zᴵ=(1/2)CᴵⱼₖV⁻¹KᴶKᴷ+Lᴵ and k=μ(dψ+A)+ω.

The imported Bena–Warner system is solved using eight harmonic functions H, hi, Mi and K. Self-dual Gi, algebraic warp factors Zi=Mi+2H⁻¹sijk hjhk, and an angular-momentum one-form encode the solution.

Regularity is studied through near-H=0 expansions, cancellation of singular metric and C-field terms, center integrability, and topology/flux integrals. Stable causality is imposed using t as a time function; the horizon argument then constructs outward timelike trajectories.

The gravitino mass matrix is obtained by reducing ten-dimensional fermionic terms, using SU(3) spinor bilinears, structure-form identities, a Majorana spinor ansatz and rescalings that normalize four-dimensional kinetic terms.

The N=1 description is extracted from the surviving gravitino mass and checked against retained-field kinetic terms. Vacua are found using Kähler-covariant F-term equations; second derivatives of the scalar potential distinguish a full minimum from a saddle.

Hidden-sector supergravity analysis, exemplified by the (3,2) theory, with W0 adjusted to nearly cancel the cosmological constant. Starting from DρW = 0, the hidden-sector potential is treated perturbatively to estimate the canonically normalized modulus mass, displacement and F term.
Soft terms are inferred from Kahler and gauge couplings, no-scale cancellations and anomaly mediation, with additional α′ corrections and low-energy loop effects considered.

The imported a-maximisation principle extremizes a cubic trial anomaly. Geometric calculations use supersymmetric-cycle volumes and the imported Z-minimisation procedure for the Reeb vector; the paper compares the resulting R-charges and central charges.

Periodic bipartite brane tilings encode gauge groups as faces, fields as edges and superpotential terms as vertices. Kasteleyn characteristic polynomials recover toric diagrams in examples, supplying an additional construction check.

GLSM quotients, homotopy sequences, Poincaré duality, line bundles and lens-space topology relate toric facets to wrapped-brane states and field charges. Flat worldvolume line bundles count distinct torsion-charged states with identical continuous global charges.

Uplift the charged Kaluza–Klein black hole, continue t → iτ and Q → iq to obtain a real Euclidean metric, remove the conical singularity by identifying τ at fixed ỹ = y − Aτ, and continue θ → π/2 + iψ to obtain the bubble spacetime.

Evaluate the Euclidean Einstein action with a flat-reference extrinsic-curvature boundary subtraction; Ricci flatness eliminates the bulk contribution. An alternative evaluation uses I = F/T, horizon entropy and a Smarr relation. The authors report agreement.
Integrate over parameters of a linear slow-roll potential using delta functions fixing N and δρ/ρ, then condition the resulting efold weighting on anthropic or observational lower bounds.

Use mass conservation R³(ρ + δρ) = M and minimize the overdense region's Friedmann equation to obtain a collapse condition. The invariant perturbation strength is defined by ρ̃ = lim δρ³/ρ²; subsequent evolution need not remain linear.
Review Coleman–De Luccia Euclidean instantons and their Lorentzian continuation; evolve the resulting scalar–FRW equations with tunneling initial conditions.

Construct a compatible Kähler structure from K and λ, then use Hodge decomposition and Hamiltonian annihilation equations. Solve the Gauss-law automorphy condition with Siegel–Narain theta functions; Poisson resummation supplies an alternative factorization construction.

Extract modular transformations from theta functions and determinant-line normalization. Use Gauss–Milgram sums and imported lattice-existence theorems to establish the invariant classification and its converse.

Treat wavefunctions as sections of a line bundle with curvature. Construct the large-gauge lifting cocycle through spin Chern–Simons phases on twisted bundles and a spin-cobordism argument, then adjust the local trivialization.

Canonical-field slow-roll estimates are combined with numerical evolution of the coupled tachyon, volume-modulus and scale-factor equations. Geometry-dependent DBI coefficients are tested against e-fold and density-perturbation requirements.

Dimensional reduction of the warped bulk and non-BPS brane actions; a KKLT-like superpotential, anti-D3 uplift proportional to X^−2, and the leading R^4-derived α′ correction supply the volume potential. Independence of the nonperturbative potential from the tachyon is argued heuristically.
Use DBI/Wess–Zumino couplings to compute induced lower-brane charges and Stückelberg couplings. The paper describes Kähler-sector RR two-forms as absorbed by U(1) gauge fields, which become massive.
Impose F^(2,0)=0 to constrain complex structure and J^3−J∧F^2=0 to constrain Kähler moduli, separately for every stack. Also require positive generalized world-volume element, F^3−J^2∧F>0.
Use the reviewed GVW superpotential W=∫G3∧Ω, with W=∂φW=∂τijW=0, together with primitivity J∧G3=0. Supersymmetric G3 must be of type (2,1); such primitive flux is imaginary self-dual.

Prepotentials are extracted by shifting the gravitino to diagonalize kinetic terms and projecting its variation onto SU(3) singlets. Finite form expansions, p-form gauge invariance and d²=0 then constrain the KK ansatz; the torsion vectors obey V_a·V_b=0.

The paper imports Hitchin's construction: use stable real Spin(6,6) spinors on the q<0 branch, their symplectic/Mukai pairing and Hamiltonian dual, then quotient by C*. The resulting local special Kähler potential is K=-ln H, with H the Hitchin function.

An M5 worldvolume coupling to the pulled-back flux produces a two-form tadpole. The authors impose i*G=0 as a necessary instanton condition, then translate it into lattice orthogonality constraints for G0.

The authors use the Künneth decomposition and integral tensor coefficients to fix the holomorphic two-planes and establish their rank-two integral lattices. Binary quadratic-form reduction bounds lattice coefficients, followed by a reported finite computer enumeration.

Proposition 1 supplies 20 embedded rational curves spanning Pic(S)⊗R and dual area coordinates. Products of K3 volumes and curve areas give 40 independent divisor-volume functions; their instanton exponentials motivate generic isolated vacua.
Expand about φ0, identify a position-dependent quadratic mass, and use a conformal field/metric transformation followed by a constant field shift to rewrite the interacting theory.
Apply Hitchin's information-metric formula to the classical solution's density, using its position and scale parameters as moduli.
Test selected field variations around φ0 and estimate vacuum decay by WKB, using a barrier action proportional to the Euclidean S4 volume times the potential-height scale.

Higher-dimensional FRW evolution is combined with energy conservation and an averaged equation of state. A randomly oriented, noninteracting gas of d-branes has w=-d/n and density ρ_d∼a^(d-n). The authors compare dilution rates to test candidate dominant components.

For interacting networks, the authors import the causal scaling logic used for cosmic strings: a horizon volume ∼t^n contains brane volume ∼t^d, giving ρ_d∼t^(d-n). This assumes maximally efficient decay and a statistically similar network at the horizon scale.

Impose metric-flux Jacobi/Bianchi identities and derive RR tadpoles from the C7 equation, including mH3+dF2. The metric contribution matters because background F2 need not be closed on the twisted torus.

Use the inherited flux superpotential W=∫e^Jc∧F_RR+∫Ωc∧(H3+dJc) with the N=1 F-term potential. Solve DΦW=0 for supersymmetric branches, additionally W=0 for Minkowski, and selected ∂ΦV=0 equations for nonsupersymmetric extrema.

Expand e^h in instanton exponentials and loop powers, solving successive inhomogeneous Laplace equations. One-instanton solutions use separation of variables and spherical Bessel functions; numerical methods analyze the truncated scalar potential.

Use the imported Przanowski–Tod description of four-dimensional quaternion-Kähler metrics with one Killing vector. Geometry is encoded by h satisfying (∂u²+∂v²)h+∂r²(e^h)=0; the surviving isometry shifts t.

Apply nonlinear Gauss–Seidel updates on uniform real-coordinate lattices, using second-order finite differences and third-order overlap interpolation. Dynamically average det g to determine the discrete normalization λ̃ and remove constant-potential drift.

Encode the metric by local scalar potentials, gi j̄=∂i∂j̄K. Holomorphic coordinate transitions prescribe complex structure; Kähler transformations on overlaps prescribe the Kähler class. Ricci-flatness becomes a second-order complex Monge–Ampère equation.

Assess continuum convergence using analytic volume normalization, integrated Euler density and Kähler-potential agreement on overlaps. A separate iterative eigenproblem computes the lowest scalar-Laplacian mode in a specified odd-parity sector.

Chiral quantization uses u=(p−x)/√2 and s=(p+x)/√2 as incoming and outgoing bases. Fourier transforms encode 0B scattering, while Bessel kernels occur in 0A. Products of one-particle amplitudes and scattering-phase densities yield transition amplitudes and thermal free energies.

The 0A calculation uses a gauged complex bifundamental matrix model with unequal ranks, a Chern-Simons coupling, and a Wilson line in a specified representation. Diagonalizing the matrix and integrating out gauge fields reduces the minimal representation sector to radial fermion dynamics.

The appendix explains a previously used tensor-reduction method: generate contractions, replace individual tensors by Young-projected forms, and simplify those forms with mono-term symmetries. This incorporates multi-term identities while avoiding expansion of full projectors.

Determine coefficients by matching integral and basis-tensor values for selected index assignments and solving a linear system. Evaluate basis contractions through vertex-by-vertex backtracking edge colouring, rejecting inconsistent assignments; naive symmetry enumeration would involve approximately (3!)^8 × 8! terms.

Count singlets in symmetrised representation products before constructing contractions. Represent antisymmetric three-index sets by trivalent vertices, delta contractions by edges, and an epsilon tensor by a ten-valent vertex. Disconnected multigraphs and multiple edges are allowed.

For equal two-charge configurations, the author constructs time-symmetric initial data using a circle-warped spherical metric with functions U and h. Choosing U and solving the scalar constraint, including three-form flux, gives a bubble mass function whose extrema identify static configurations.

Static charged bubbles are constructed by double analytic continuation t→iχ and x→it. Smoothness fixes the χ period. Proposed endpoints are constrained by conservation of charge and asymptotic circle size and by matching the transverse horizon and bubble sizes.

Truncates the hypermultiplet metric under the orientifold, introduces corrected complex coordinates to express it as Kähler, and compares the N=1 F-term potential with the projected N=2 gauged potential.

Uses the Przanowski–Tod description of four-dimensional quaternion-Kähler metrics with at least one Killing vector. The metric is determined by a function satisfying the three-dimensional Toda equation, with perturbative and leading membrane-instanton solutions imported from [9].

Dimensionally reduce curvature-quartic terms on the zeroth-order product metric, retain two-derivative scalar kinetic terms and rescale to four-dimensional Einstein frame to extract the Kähler correction.

Extremize the axionic combination analytically, then study extrema in orbifold length numerically. The displayed example uses |h|=10⁻⁸, visible-boundary volume 800 and hidden-sector dual Coxeter number 8.
Solve corrected Killing-spinor equations together with the G-field equation and Bianchi identity. For the specified flat-external-space background, G∧G and X₈ vanish through order κ^{4/3}.

Order-of-magnitude estimates combine radiation density ρ_R ∼ T⁴ with the black-hole scaling T² ∼ M_pl⁻²ρ, giving ρ_R ∼ M_pl⁻⁴ρ². Replacing the density by ρ − ρ_R heuristically motivates a negative quadratic-density correction to the temperature relation.

The de Sitter relation T ∼ H motivates transferring the temperature correction to the Friedmann equation. For the bounce calculation, the authors expand the density and scale factor near the proposed bounce and solve a first-order equation for x = a(t) − a(t_p).

Construct the holomorphic three-form Ω and determine its discrete transformation. Enumerate independent polynomial deformations after removing coordinate redefinitions, then use their transformation properties to identify fluxes that preserve the symmetry. The relevant flux transformation differs from that of its paired scalar modulus.

Gepner minimal-model state charges and the supersymmetry operator provide a second identification of R transformations and a check of deformation counting. Flux-space dimension reduction is then used as a heuristic indicator of vacuum-number suppression.

Expand S and z^i in both x=C exp(-aT) and its conjugate through quadratic order. The resulting ansatz is G=ln(v+b x+bar b bar x+c x^2+bar c bar x^2+d|x|^2+...)-3ln(T+bar T), with coefficients depending on integer fluxes.

Solve heavy-field Kähler-derivative conditions with the nonperturbative term already present, substitute their generally nonholomorphic solutions into G=K+ln|W|^2, and compute the bosonic scalar potential from G. Retaining the induced complex-structure Kähler contribution is essential to the argument.
Use Laguerre eigenfunctions and spectral sums for the partition function and propagator. Differentiate the partition function with respect to couplings to obtain hole number and spacetime volume.
Exact combinatorial enumeration at fixed boundary lengths, followed by generating functions and an explicit genus sum expressed through the Catalan generating function.

Expand the transfer-matrix composition law near critical couplings. Require a delta-function at leading order, a lower-bounded Hamiltonian and independence from higher-order scaling coefficients; inverse Laplace transformation gives the spatial-length representation.
Analyze boundary variations after adding 4d(A∧B), the Gibbons–Hawking term and a chirally dressed fermionic boundary term. A boundary spinor projector selects the preserved supersymmetries.

Split auxiliary forms into temporal and spatial components, integrate out nondynamical fields and solve the resulting constraints. In the on-shell variant, a chiral gravitino redefinition exposes the residual boundary action.
Lift the deck transformations of flat three-manifolds to Spin(3), impose spinor equivariance, and test whether a flat chiral connection cancels spin holonomy.

Construct the supergravity F-term potential, locate stationary points, diagonalize the Hessian with the stated field-space normalization, and numerically integrate the two-field equations using elapsed e-folds N as time.

Use a quadratic tachyonic-saddle approximation and exponential growth ansatz to estimate N≈ln(φ*/φ0)/|ηs|. Reduce the inflationary trajectory to an asymmetric one-dimensional double well and estimate wall thicknesses from gradient–potential energy balance.

Represent polynomial observables as multiplication operators on C[φ]/⟨∂iW⟩. Their eigenvalues are critical-point values, and traces of powers yield holomorphic moments without explicitly locating every critical point.

Use dimensions and residual discrete symmetries to restrict moment formulas. Compute small-interaction coefficients by reductions involving finitely many variables or equivalent diagrammatic counting; resultants diagnose failure of generic root counting.
Estimate Wilsonian loop corrections to the Kähler potential and metric. Coordinate-invariant trace and determinant bounds constrain the large-N sizes of superpotential and Kähler tensors.

Generalized tangent-bundle invariance supplies the geometric interpretation. Spinor norm inequalities produce the calibration bound; twisted closure and a chain deformation argument give the associated integrated energy-minimization statement.

The authors reduce the D-brane κ-symmetry projector using a four-plus-six-dimensional spinor decomposition, then expand the internal conditions in a spinor basis. Clifford maps and Fierz identities express the resulting equations through pure-spinor differential forms.

Two- and three-point functions, reflection-covariant structure constants, and alternative OPE factorizations supplement the chiral equations. The flow-violating three-point structure constant is matched to an ordinary Liouville vertex up to an undetermined k-dependent factor.

The author inserts a flowed-current null-vector equation, expresses current modes through contour integrals and Ward identities, and applies a correlator twist κ. Sklyanin separation of variables then converts the surviving KZ combinations into BPZ equations.

Instead of calculating a broken-supersymmetry Casimir potential first, the authors infer ΔK from one-loop corrections to the radion kinetic term and four-dimensional Einstein term at W=0. Dimensional arguments are applied before Weyl rescaling, using the absence of the higher-dimensional Planck mass from these one-loop terms.

Matching the Einstein-frame radion kinetic term to K=−3ln(T+T̄) fixes the relation between R and Re T. The corrected Kähler potential is then inserted into the standard supergravity scalar-potential formula after introducing a small constant W; the potential is also expressed in the original metric frame.

Higher-dimensional correspondence is assessed by matching reduced effective actions: circle-reduced O3/O7 theories against M-theory on selected fourfolds, and O6 theories against selected G2 compactifications.
Massless chiral/linear multiplet dualization uses a Legendre transform. In the appendix conventions, K=K̃−2(Tκ+T̄κ)Lκ and Tλ=iξ̃λ+(1/4)∂LλK̃, with L determined implicitly.

Kaluza-Klein expansion in harmonic forms, orientifold parity truncation and Weyl rescaling produce the bosonic action; comparison with standard N=1 supergravity identifies Kähler potentials and holomorphic gauge couplings.

The potential is identified from the four-dimensional tt Einstein constraint after dropping velocities, then integrated over the compact space and converted to four-dimensional Einstein normalization.

Linearized Einstein, three-form, five-form and axidilaton equations organize spacetime-dependent perturbations. Harmonic forms and Lichnerowicz eigenfunctions distinguish zero modes from Kaluza–Klein modes; scalar Green functions determine warp-factor and brane-source responses.

The proper-time integral is performed using a Bessel representation and its large-argument approximation, equivalently Laplace's method. Functional stationary phase then uses S=m√(∫₀¹du ẋ²)+ie∫₀¹du A·ẋ.

Changing variable from position to the scaled gauge potential yields a unified action quadrature involving √(1−y²)/|f′|. The authors identify it with the standard WKB exponential; selected spatial rates additionally use imported WKB prefactors.

The saddle equations imply constant speed ẋ²=a². For one-coordinate potentials they reduce to integrable equations; elementary functions solve pulse/bump examples and Jacobi elliptic functions solve sinusoidal examples. Periodicity fixes a and winding number.

Use dimensional reduction and the Einstein-frame gravitino variation to test effective potentials. In the nearly Kähler specialization, compare curvature characteristic forms for a one-parameter family of torsionful connections to address the H Bianchi identity.
Set the ten-dimensional fermion supersymmetry variations to zero; decompose the supersymmetry spinor, use Fierz and gamma-matrix identities, and extract intrinsic torsion classes from dJ and dΩ.

Rewrite collective motion using ρ²=Σnφ²n and apply slow-roll dynamics. For unequal masses, approximate a dense logarithmic spectrum by a continuous field label and estimate the duration and amplitude loss during critical damping.

Use shift-symmetry power counting and supergravity F-term analysis for potential corrections; estimate species corrections through dimensional reduction of a ten-dimensional R⁴ term and naive dimensional analysis of string loops.

The appendix studies general gauge-invariant actions in F, A=P−C, and derivatives. Constant-source response and the zero-momentum behavior of inverse differential operators distinguish potential contributions from derivative terms.

Dualize by treating P=dB as independent, imposing its Bianchi identity with axion a as Lagrange multiplier, and eliminating P and C through their equations of motion. The arbitrary potential is related to the three-form kinetic function K through the inverse of K′; κ arises as an integration constant.

Dimensional reduction is expressed in special Kähler variables z^I=A^I/√3+i h_tilde^I/√2, with h_tilde^I=e^σ h^I. A cubic prepotential, Kähler potential and period matrix encode the reduced bosonic Lagrangian.

Unification is tested through subgroup branchings of the symplectic electric–magnetic representation, seeking a real irreducible electric half. Unified gauging further requires all electric vectors to form the adjoint representation of a simple gauge group. Graded Jordan conformal algebras and representation dimensions constrain possible hidden symmetries.

The reviewed five-dimensional construction encodes the theory in a constant symmetric tensor C_IJK: V(h)=C_IJK h^I h^J h^K, a_IJ=−(1/3)∂_I∂_J ln V, with scalar manifold V=1. The scalar metric is the appropriately normalized pullback of a_IJ.

Expand the ten-dimensional Einstein action and probe-brane Born–Infeld/RR action, canonically normalizing fields. The resulting interaction φKK(∂Ŷ)²/Λ gives ΓKK = mKK³√(1−4μ²/mKK²)/(32πΛ²), subject to the decay threshold.

Estimate KK thermalization with τ ∼ 1/(nσv), convert energy densities into thermal temperatures, and use cosmological freeze-out estimates for angular KK relics. These are approximate kinetic estimates.

Approximate localized KK spectra using a massless-scalar eigenmode equation, H ≃ e^(4y), and effectively constant throat radius R. Transformation to Bessel functions gives a mass gap of order e^(−y0)/R.

Vary the world-sheet action in Kähler coordinates to construct adapted vertex operators. Because these coordinates mix open and closed scalars, their vertices contain both boundary and bulk contributions.

Extract kinetic metrics from the coefficient linear in δ=p1·p2 after relaxing momentum conservation, then integrate to a Kähler potential. A specific four-point annulus calculation tests the moduli dependence of this prescription without momentum relaxation.

Compute annulus, Möbius-strip and Klein-bottle two-point amplitudes using spin-structure sums, the method of images, Chan–Paton traces and lattice sums. Regulated integrals produce generalized Eisenstein series; tadpole cancellation removes the displayed UV cutoff terms.

Classify supersymmetric, Lorentz-scalar UV perturbations using the imported AdS₅×T¹,¹ KK spectrum and superconformal multiplets. Analyze diagonal F- and D-flat probe branches to exclude superpotential deformations incompatible with a six-dimensional geometric moduli space.

Propagate UV perturbations with φ(u)=a u^(−Δ)+b u^(Δ−4), estimate IR suppression, and infer angular masses from the perturbed warp factor and probe kinetic term. The orientifold alternative uses a previously computed flat-space Möbius-strip amplitude.

Test discrete isometry quotients through fixed points and shrinking cycles; use coordinate rescalings to expose BTZ normalization ambiguity and the global Gauss–Bonnet theorem to constrain compact hyperbolic horizons.

Analyze stationary coordinate changes t_s = λt + f(r,x), observe that the spacetime determinant loses its dependence on f, and use translations of infinitesimal spacetime strips along Killing orbits to argue slicing independence after fixing time normalization.

Determine superpotential coefficients using topological T-duality rules and coordinate permutations. Exchanging Greek and Latin coordinate roles in IIB exchanges constant/cubic and linear/quadratic τ terms. The IIB construction uses transformations explicit for individual fluxes; completing IIA requires the formal R extension.

Use generalized Scherk–Schwarz reductions with SL(2,R) monodromy matrices to obtain coordinate-dependent R–R field strengths and integrated Bianchi constraints. Derive general constraints by T-duality and identify NS–NS constraints with Jacobi identities of a generalized gauge algebra.

Estimate inter-throat energy transfer using localized KK-graviton tunnelling in an AdS proxy: Γt scales as n⁴e^(5Ainf)/R. Treat tunnelling as the bottleneck and estimate an EFT temperature Trh ∼ √(Γt MP).
Combine supergravity cross-couplings with de Sitter scalar fluctuations and self-interactions to motivate Hubble-induced effective masses, then interpret the throat deformation modulus geometrically.
Use imported exponential open-string length distributions, interaction rates and polarization-dependent decay rates, followed by coupled continuity equations for strings and radiation.

For lattice constructions, begin at Γ(22,6)=Γ(19,3)⊕Γ(3,3), use Nikulin's classification of K3-related symplectic automorphisms and Niemeier's lattice enumeration, then combine permutations of identical component root lattices with torus shifts.

Fermionic current algebra constructions impose modular invariance, Verlinde fusion rules and the worldsheet supersymmetry triplet constraint. Allowed Z2-twisted Majorana blocks begin with sizes 16, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44 and 48; these restrictions organize gauge-rank reduction and the exotic examples.

Use Killing-potential identities and gauge invariance to constrain D-terms and W; analyze extrema and stability of the real-scalar potential V(s), then assess additional-field extrema through factorization and scalar mass-mixing conditions.

After imposing D_SW=D_UW=0, expand in inverse volume and seek minima in A and ρ. The retained schematic potential is V=|W|²r⁻³[c₁r⁻³ᐟ²+c₂r⁻²+…], with r=−i(ρ−ρ̄); coefficients depend on A and the flux-fixed leading values of S and U.

Insert the corrected Kähler potential into the N=1 F-term potential. Combine the known sphere α′ correction with Klein-bottle, annulus and Möbius-strip one-loop contributions; the latter are expressed through nonholomorphic lattice sums E₂(A,U).

Represent the remaining polynomial by a real symmetric matrix G. Standard Green–Schwarz factorization requires rank at most two; at rank two its nonzero eigenvalues must have opposite signs. Product groups additionally require compatible root choices across the coupled pairwise equalities.

Supplement local cancellation with global gauge-anomaly integrality constraints. The review identifies G2, SU(3) and SU(2) as the simple groups with nontrivial sixth homotopy groups, respectively Z3, Z6 and Z12, and includes an additional condition for gauged Sp(1)_R.

Sum chiral-field anomaly eight-forms and reduce representation traces to fundamental traces using coefficients a, b and c. Remove irreducible terms by imposing n_H−n_V=273−29n_T and A_α=0 for each independent quartic gauge invariant.

Bessel-function KK wavefunctions and a one-dimensional Schrödinger barrier describe localization and tunneling. Israel matching and IR Z2 boundary conditions give P∼(mR)^4 and Γ_tunn∼(mR)^4/|z_i| for mR≪1; an appendix includes reflection from the receiving throat.

Compare collision times (nσv)^−1, thermalization, tunneling, brane decay and Hubble expansion. After matter-like dilution, reheating is estimated at H∼τ_tunn^−1, with T_RH∼g_*^−1/4(M_Pl/τ_tunn)^1/2 and g_*∼100.

Perturbative flat-space worldsheet decay rates are averaged over initial oscillator states at fixed level N and summed over final levels and allowed radial KK modes. Finite-N effects are retained, while state degeneracies use a large-N approximation. Squared warped wavefunctions then estimate curved-throat enhancement.

Integrated Einstein equations and flux Bianchi identities produce no-go and tadpole constraints. In IIB, ND3−NO3/4+Nflux=0, with Nflux=∫H3∧F3/[(2π)^4 α′²]; the stated F-theory relation is ND3+Nflux=χ(X4)/24. Such charge constraints do not bound every individual flux: the displayed IIA example allows arbitrary F2, F4 and F6 after fixing F0H3.

Decompose gravitino and dilatino supersymmetry conditions into internal-spinor and SU(3) representations, relating fluxes, warp factor and intrinsic torsion classes. Compatible pure spinors on T⊕T* provide the generalized-geometric formulation.

Kaluza–Klein reduction retains a finite set of light modes, using harmonic forms for Calabi–Yau compactifications. The resulting N=1 potential is expressed through K, W and D-terms; gravitino variations are also used to obtain flux superpotentials.

Evaluate the N=1 F-term potential using nonperturbative W and K=Kcs−2 ln(V+ξ/2), including the stated α′ correction. Minimize other small-cycle moduli at fixed V, then compare volume potentials with and without the inflaton's stabilizing contribution.

Canonical normalization precedes differentiation of the inflationary potential. The authors compute slow-roll parameters and the e-fold integral, numerically solve the parameter relations, and impose the historical COBE density-perturbation normalization.

Define off-shell vertices by punctured disks with local coordinates and CFT correlators. The BPZ pairing and three-string vertex determine the star product, geometrically represented by overlapping complementary half-strings.

Use conformal minimal-area metrics to construct moduli-space cells: nontrivial open curves have length at least π, closed curves at least 2π. Jenkins–Strebel differentials supply the open construction and genus-zero closed construction; higher-genus closed foliations can cross.

Handle infinitely reducible gauge symmetry with BV fields and antifields packaged into one unrestricted-ghost-number, Grassmann-odd string field. The classical master action retains Witten's cubic form.
Hidden-sector dimensional transmutation supplies ⟨λλ⟩=Λ³, with Λ approximately μ exp[-1/(b0 g²(μ))]. Gaugino condensation is represented by a nonperturbative superpotential term C exp(-af).

The analysis uses the supergravity scalar potential and approximate condition DXW≈0, canonical normalization of modulus fluctuations, and a perturbative estimate of displacement under T-dependent uplifting to infer the modulus mass and suppressed F-term.

Identify cohomological representatives of massless matter fields, determine the relevant dimensions, and translate them into field counts. Separate this calculation for one manifold from the stronger problem of bounding counts across a family.

Compare universal properties of known ultraviolet constructions with the larger set allowed by semiclassical reasoning. Test gravity dependence by decoupling gravity, then formulate conjectures and seek an independent obstruction for candidate theories lacking constructions.

Assume the existence of a bulk electrically charged one-brane, determine its worldvolume theory, and test that theory's consistency. A contradiction could constrain the bulk candidate only after the existence assumption and worldvolume analysis are justified.
Restrict scalar integration to the region with E≪Λ and all integrated-out masses m≫Λ. Compute metric volume there and track its cutoff dependence before discussing the Λ→0 limit.

Translate the gravitational conjecture through AdS/CFT, then compare the resulting question with known conformal-field-theory examples. Use the independent worldsheet identification of geometric moduli as a consistency check.

Reduce uncertainty from unexamined constructions by studying higher-dimensional theories with fewer internal geometric choices. The paper contrasts this with lower-dimensional compactifications, where geometry, flux and brane data produce a much larger search space.

Collective coordinates are counted by index theorems; overlap integrals of gauge-fixed zero modes define moduli-space metrics. Lifting solitons to higher dimensions promotes collective coordinates to worldvolume fields and clarifies supersymmetry pairing.

Bogomolny completion of squares gives first-order soliton equations and topological action, mass or tension bounds. Dimensional reduction relates self-duality to monopole equations and vortex equations to wall equations.

ADHM realizes instanton data as the hyperKähler quotient of an auxiliary U(k) theory with adjoint and fundamental hypermultiplets. Nahm uses interval matrix data with impurity or pole boundary conditions to encode monopoles.

The two-step strategy computes a finite-volume UV approximation to the moduli-space metric and then argues that RG evolution preserves finiteness. Free-field two-point functions of OI = P Zi1 Zi2 Zi3 Zi4 Zi5 give the UV metric on the superpotential coefficients.

Symplectic reduction selects representatives of complexified field-redefinition orbits. The construction first removes the overall GL(1) rescaling, producing CP125, and then takes the remaining SL(5) quotient. The UV metric is restricted to representatives of the physical moduli.

Use string mass-shell and level-matching conditions to calculate species energies, then model the gas by ρ = Σs ñs Es and directional pressures derived from changes of total energy with scale factors. Apply dimensional reduction and conformal transformations to examine physical stabilization in Einstein frame.

Obtain background equations from worldsheet beta functions and their low-energy spacetime action; add the string sigma-model action as a matter source and average individual string stress tensors into a gas.

Treat additional light string modes near enhanced symmetry as fields with time-dependent masses. Estimate nonadiabatic production, occupation numbers and energy density, then include their backreaction and Hubble damping in radion evolution.

In the type I dual, a sector of 16 D9-branes and eight anti-D9-branes supplies a real tachyon. A fourth-Hopf-map configuration, smoothed near a ray and the origin, constructs a semi-infinite D1-brane.

The Atiyah–Singer index on S8 and the SO(32) adjoint/vector trace relation give a 24-mode spacetime mismatch, matching the world-sheet count 32−8. A four-dimensional index argument extends mode matching to monopole junctions.
Use supersymmetric gauged linear sigma models, Fayet–Iliopoulos running, Landau–Ginzburg/hybrid phases and adjunction to construct UV completions flowing toward Riemann-surface sigma models.

Compare curvature-induced and supercritical string-frame potentials; apply the Selberg trace formula to winding-state density and one-loop modular transformations to its required infrared counterpart.

The holographic arguments use a cutoff thermofield description, bulk propagator estimates, and analytic continuation. Heavy-operator two-point functions are approximated by exp(−mL), with radial spacelike geodesics matched across a transparent wall and continued toward null limits.

Israel junction conditions reduce shell motion to a zero-energy effective-potential problem. Extrinsic-curvature signs select admissible spacetime patches. Initial-value constraints and domains of dependence support the smooth scalar-gravity construction; Raychaudhuri focusing supplies the causal-disconnection argument.

Calculate instanton actions using the axion's dual nine-form description, scalar boundary terms, the Gibbons–Hawking term and AdS counterterms. The appendix derives the effective wrong-sign axion equations from a momentum-boundary-state path integral and dualization.

Organize radial solutions using the SL(2,R) Noether-charge matrix, its invariant determinant and a harmonic function on the deformed geometry. Analyze the two non-extremal signs separately and change radial coordinates to expose the wormhole neck.

Expand massless scalar fields near the Poincaré boundary and obtain one-point functions by varying the on-shell action with respect to boundary sources. Use the z4 coefficients for dimension-four operators even though a compact bulk harmonic function is unavailable in D = 5.

Review the FMW spectral-cover/Fourier–Mukai construction and use Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch for Chern data. Form U(n) bundles V ⊗ Q by line-bundle twisting; the imported stability result says twisting preserves μ-stability in both directions.

Determine perturbative matter through bundle cohomology and net chirality through Euler characteristics. Describe five-brane matter using coherent sheaves and global Ext groups; the mixed bundle/five-brane chiral index is −∫X c1(Vi) ∧ γa.

Analyze the scalar responsible for spontaneous CP breaking in the presence of a positive brane-localized mass. An energy estimate and a stated exact wall profile give the suppression of its brane value relative to its bulk value.

For field-dependent brane charge, couple C to the transverse projection of the membrane current. The appendix introduces a compensating two-form Stückelberg field and a two-form Lagrange multiplier, then integrates them out to obtain the projected coupling from a local gauge-invariant formulation.

Integrate the static planar-wall field equation across the wall to obtain a flux jump, then estimate vacuum counts by integrating inverse charge over flux. For illustrating accumulation, take a quadratic K(F), while claiming that the attractor's existence does not depend on its detailed form.

Uses quasi-projective compactification and resolution of the boundary divisor to normal crossings. Near an intersection, punctured-disk coordinates describe the complement of the divisor; explicit blowups resolve the Argyres–Douglas cusp.

Uses quasi-unipotent monodromy, finite covers and Schmid’s nilpotent-orbit theorem to expand periods, with N^4=0 for threefolds. Special-geometry identities then reduce index-growth estimates to power counting of e^K, Yukawa couplings and inverse metrics.

Imports the Ashok–Douglas signed-index formula, schematically det(R+ω), associated with the top Chern form of Ω_M^{1,0}⊗L^{-1}. The full expression includes signs and 2π factors; the density relation is proportional, without a fixed overall normalization here.

Under the restricted matter ansatz, use W=A+BS, or constant W0 after integrating out S. Analyze special parameter choices analytically and exhibit a numerical minimum when D3 matter has a nonzero vev.
Construct the scalar potential from supergravity F terms and flux-induced Fayet–Iliopoulos plus charged-matter D terms, using the lowest-order matter expansion of the Kähler potential.

Introduce a formal rescaling e^φ → λe^φ and C_(p) → λ^−1 C_(p), with an accompanying brane-coordinate rescaling, so S → S/λ² and G^r → λ^−1 G^r. Flux ratios are λ independent; the authors use this homogeneity to exclude loop corrections to W in the reorganized expansion.

Promote background flux values to transforming spurions G^r. R charge and holomorphy constrain W locally to G^0 w(ϕ^i; G^r/G^0); PQ invariance excludes separate τ dependence of w. The tree-level GVW expression is linear in the flux spurions.

Extend the leading-α′ result using holomorphy and form-field shift symmetries: W cannot acquire Kähler-modulus dependence, while cycle volumes entering the α′ expansion belong to those moduli. The authors infer absence of perturbative α′ corrections.

The cosmological estimate follows [13]: approximate a tachyonic direction by V=V0-m² phi²/2, apply fast-roll evolution, and impose the imported quantum-fluctuation floor phi0 approximately at least m/C, with C=O(10).

Compute the supergravity F-term potential, use s_i=exp[sqrt(2/(3a_i)) phi_i] to normalize the saxions, and diagonalize the normalized Hessian. The spectral calculation uses a rank-one matrix structure, orthogonal subspaces, and a remaining two-dimensional block.
Solve h·Π(x₀)=0 and f·Π,ᵢ(x₀)−τ₀h·Π,ᵢ(x₀)=0, compute W₀=f·Π(x₀), then choose racetrack parameters to impose W=∂ρW=0. The example uses a period expansion in ψ².

Express first and second derivatives of the F-term potential through the complex gravitino mass and chiral fermion mass matrix; specialize to supersymmetric Minkowski conditions and factorize the mixed Hessian using the inverse Kähler metric.

For a rolling scalar, use a classical solution to express φ and its energy density as functions of a, requiring monotonic a(t). Constant-equation-of-state scaling solutions then reduce the problem to an effective scale-factor WDW equation.

Solve the Wheeler–DeWitt equation semiclassically, matching oscillatory and exponential WKB solutions across turning points. The barrier exponent is estimated geometrically and evaluated using complete elliptic integrals and numerical maximization; WKB prefactors are neglected.

Apply linear scalar cosmological perturbation theory and the sub-Hubble Einstein constraint ∇²Φ = 4πGδρ to convert thermal matter fluctuations into metric fluctuations at mode exit. Propagate the result through the transition using assumptions about super-Hubble conservation.

Use the thermal partition function Z(β) = Σ_i exp(−βE_i) in finite regions. At fixed volume, the canonical energy variance gives ⟨(δM)²⟩ = T²C_V, relating mass fluctuations to the string gas specific heat.
Assess thermal destabilization through ΔV=(α0+α2 g²)T_b⁴, where T_b is temperature and α2 is positive in most cases; compare its modulus dependence for f=mS±wT.

Analyze supergravity F-term extrema satisfying D_T W=0, add V_L=D/(T+T̄)^np, and tune the total vacuum energy to zero. A small displacement from the SUSY AdS extremum estimates F^T and modulus masses.

Use the production of entanglement as an operational indicator of interaction, and interaction as a proposed indicator of spacetime coincidence. The approach is inspired by an Everett-style account in which measurements are unitary processes increasing correlations between subsystems.

Search over alternative TPSs rather than only subsets of predetermined lattice sites. For a given state, the proposed selection principle minimizes the tendency to create entanglement across this wider, infinite family of possible factorizations.
For the two F₀ phases, the authors use Picard–Lefschetz transformations and an SL(2,Z) basis change to relate wrapped-cycle charges and identify Seiberg duality.

Weighted Kasteleyn determinants and perfect-matching winding numbers describe the spectral polynomial. Euler characteristic and Pick's theorem relate untwisted graph topology to toric area and interior lattice points.

Logarithmic-modulus and angular projections define amoebae and algae. Asymptotic two-monomial limits identify winding cycles; Monte Carlo sampling plots alga interiors when explicit parametrizations are unavailable.
Use slow-roll field relations, moments of the mass distribution, multifield e-fold derivatives for adiabatic perturbations, and numerical integration of background equations.
Approximate the leading mass matrix by the Gram form M = RᵀR and apply the imported Marčenko–Pastur spectral law to a rectangular random matrix.

Monte Carlo simulations assemble component matrices using the supergravity mass formula and varied input distributions. The simulated Kähler metrics are random symmetric positive-definite proxies rather than explicit compactification metrics.

Compare corrected and uncorrected stationary points and η numerically across L and a scaling parameter λ. The uncorrected benchmark gives η = −0.0061, which the authors report agrees with the original racetrack calculation.

Insert the corrected Kähler potential and metric into the supergravity F-term potential, examine stationary points, and evaluate inflationary curvature with the noncanonical inflaton kinetic term included. At a stationary saddle ε = 0; the stated curvature prescription is η = VYY/(2gTT̄ V).
Establish the required spectral-line-bundle existence through degeneration to a reducible curve, analysis of its Picard group, non-torsion extension classes, and a stated semicontinuity argument.

Compute bundle cohomology using long exact sequences, the index theorem, and Serre duality. A cup product with the extension class becomes an explicit 18 × 17 matrix whose rank controls Higgs multiplicities.
Construct rank-two and rank-three bundles using Fourier–Mukai transforms of spectral data, pullbacks, and line-bundle twists, then form a rank-five extension.
Describe Yukawa couplings through the normalized overlap (1/9)∫X̃ Ω∧Tr(Ψi∧Ψj∧Ψk). Nonvanishing requires the three one-form legs to span the two elliptic-fiber directions and the base direction.

Use equivariant Serre constructions with ideal sheaves of three and six points. The six-point sheaf uses multiplicity-two fixed-point support; nonfree actions on the base surfaces permit these smaller orbits.
Determine zero modes by computing Z3 × Z3 representations on bundle cohomology, tensoring with Wilson-line representations, and retaining the jointly invariant subspace.

For translation Goldstones they introduce L(p,q)=L_IJ(p)(Aq)^I(Aq)^J and use L(p,q)-L(q,p)=[p²T(q,q)-q²T(p,p)]/2. Positivity-cone arguments connect this identity to NEC. In higher dimensions, conditions derived using collinear particles are necessary but not sufficient for stability.

The authors analyze roots of det L(ω,k)=0 and use the Källén–Lehmann representation to associate eigenvalue-slope signs with propagator residues and physical particle branches. Their stability test excludes complex frequencies and multiparticle energy-momenta inside the lower light cone in an admissible quantization.

Glue resolved patches through linear divisor relations connecting inherited Ri, fixed-locus Diα, and exceptional Ek. Cover-to-quotient multiplicities matter; exceptional coefficients depend on the singularity. These relations provide input for the later intersection-ring calculation.

Resolve local abelian orbifold singularities using toric lattice rays and fan triangulations; determine exceptional-divisor topology from stars of cones. The local C3/Z6-II example has five triangulations related by birational transformations, including flops.
Combine a weight-one current with an opposite-chirality spacetime derivative and a null plane wave, then impose physical-state consistency.
Choose lattice charges and oscillator levels satisfying level matching, then compare masses.

Iteratively form attractive bound states, assume their ratios continue decreasing, and compare their masses with charge-conserving fragments. The paper extrapolates this construction into the black-hole regime.
Substitute the stated mass and coupling relations into the electric bound.
Select the charge-dependent extremality branch and minimize the allowed oscillator contribution.
Interpret the electric object of a zero-form as an instanton and substitute g ∼ 1/F.
Construct an exponential, test mutual locality against all integral-charge factors, and invoke spectrum completeness. Alternatively use the source's unit-spectral-flow argument.
Count charge sectors at fixed black-hole mass, test available discharge channels, and identify the remnant multiplicity if charge remains after evaporation.
Compare magnetic field energy or monopole compactness with a gravitational bound.

Estimate exterior field energy, associate a core scale, and compare with either magnetic extremality or the gravitational radius. The two tests share mass and size estimates but require different additional premises.
Track the same large-N limit in the gauge and gravitational sectors.

Hold conserved Q_e,Q_m fixed, perturb the black-hole fields, and tune the mass to the horizon threshold. Only afterward compare sectors or take a large-charge limit at fixed coefficients and direction.
Translate the required operator into the N_L = 0 mass formula.
Insert compactification scalings and change to a dual description at the edge of validity.
Estimate stretched-string masses and compare them with compactification-dependent gauge-gravity scales.
Reject the formulation using stated string examples and charge-conserving decay kinematics.
Compare reduced kinetic terms and the inflationary hierarchy with the validity scale of the compactification.
Background propagation and scattering-dispersion arguments are reported from another work.

Use η=(number of participating real fluxes)/(number of real moduli) as a heuristic diagnostic: η>1 suggests broad tunability, η≈1 restricted tuning, and η<1 insufficient freedom to fix all moduli. This is an expectation, not a general stabilization theorem.

Count flux choices and moduli satisfying F-flatness using delta functions, with a step function imposing the D3 tadpole bound. Replace the flux lattice sum by an integral and change to coordinates built from W and its covariant derivatives.

Review GVW flux stabilization of complex structure and axio-dilaton, followed by no-scale-breaking corrections for Kähler moduli. The illustrative one-modulus superpotential is W=W0+A exp(−aσ), representing instantons or gaugino condensation.
Define DBI Hubble parameters εD=2Mp²(H′/H)²/γ, ηD=2Mp²H″/(γH), and κD=2Mp²H′γ′/(γ²H). These definitions generalize the slow-roll framework without requiring γ≈1.

Use monotonic φ as a clock and solve Hamilton–Jacobi background equations: V=3Mp²H²−T(γ−1), γ=√(1+4Mp⁴H′²/T), and φ̇=−2Mp²H′/γ. Analytic limiting solutions provide boundary conditions for intermediate-regime numerics.

Numerically vary background and potential parameters, integrate Ne=−∫Hγ dφ/(2Mp²H′), and enforce the historical COBE amplitude δH≈1.9×10⁻⁵ at 55 e-folds before the end. The remaining parameters generate ranges of observables.

Classify stabilization effects through the four-dimensional supersymmetric potential built from K and W. The locality heuristic compares local energy growing at most as vol(X) with the Einstein-frame potential rescaling by vol(X)^(-2).

Dimensionally reduce flux energies, count inverse-metric and internal-volume factors, and Weyl-rescale to four-dimensional Einstein frame. For dimensionless metric moduli with kinetic coefficient M_P² and generic quadratic potential scale V_0, canonical normalization gives m approximately sqrt(V_0)/M_P.
A flat-torus compactification argument motivates using the same inequality m ≤ g/√G in lower dimensions, assuming consistency survives dimensional reduction.

For the dipole, the authors solve static conformal-gauge field equations, metric constraints and the Maxwell equation, then match the interior and exterior solutions using delta-function endpoint sources.
The 3D arguments use the conical deficit generated by a massive particle and, separately, Einstein-equation trace and action scaling to estimate an instanton's gravitational size.

Reduces the phase dependence to a cosine of one combination of Im T and arg M, then numerically minimizes the remaining potential. The authors report a Hessian analysis in all four real variables for their displayed example.
Uses the supergravity F/D scalar potential, Kähler derivatives, gauge invariance and an imported analytic charged-invariant criterion sufficient for simultaneous D-term cancellation.

Uses the constant-curvature equation 2f(R) − Rf′(R) = 0, de Sitter and power-law FRW ansätze, constant-w matter conservation, and effective density/pressure definitions that move curvature contributions into fluid variables.

Introduces auxiliary fields A and B and a conformal transformation with σ = −ln f′(A) to express metric f(R) gravity in an Einstein-frame scalar description. Also discusses the inverse construction from scalar–tensor models.
Tests the proposed energy bound using time-symmetric SO(3) × SO(2) initial data: choose α(r), solve the scalar constraint for β(r), and compare the resulting energies at fixed boundary circle size.

Constructs large-radius expansions containing logarithms and two interior-dependent constants C1 and C2. Numerical solutions and derivatives are matched to these expansions to extract the constants and the Hamiltonian background-subtracted energy.

Reduces the Einstein equations for radial functions α, β and γ to a third-order nonlinear ODE for α. Other metric functions follow from subsidiary equations. Smoothness at an origin or bubble, together with asymptotic normalization, selects the numerical solutions.

Approximate four-dimensional supergravity stabilization uses a flux superpotential, open-membrane instanton exponentials, Kähler-covariant equations DT_i W = DY_I W = 0, and anomalous-U(1) FI contributions to the scalar potential.

Axion winding is identified through dualization and dimensional reduction of H couplings: open membranes source σ winding, wrapped five-branes source the appropriate Kähler axion p, and solitonic strings wind the charged matter phase φ.
Monopole pair nucleation is modeled by a hole in the Euclidean string worldsheet, with action m times boundary length minus μ times removed area; the stated circular saddle has radius m/μ.

For isotropic Minkowski vacua, changes variables to U = −iρ, S = −iσ, T = −iτ and writes W = E1 + σE2 + τE3 + στE4. The analyzed elimination reduces the conditions to a double complex root of E = E1E4 − E2E3, together with flux constraints.

Uses an extended algebra of six ZM and six XM generators, with fluxes as structure constants, to obtain Bianchi constraints from Jacobi identities. S-duality closure then motivates P·P, mixed Q/P, and Q·H3 − P·F3 constraints.

Builds superpotentials as integrals of fluxes contracted with complexified geometric forms. The contractions with metric flux ω, Q and R change form degree by +1, −1 and −3, respectively; duality matching also guides proposed RR-form tadpole couplings.
Riemann–Roch–Hirzebruch indices determine bundle-associated spectra; skyscraper sheaves and Ext groups incorporate the SO(32) five-brane sector.
Toy bundles are constructed through monads or exact sequences on complete-intersection K3 realizations; intersection forms give Chern characters, DUY equations and Kähler-domain conditions.
Dimensional reduction of ten-dimensional kinetic and one-loop couplings involving B^(2) and its dual B^(6), followed by comparison with six-dimensional anomaly eight-forms.

Combine fixed-point linearization with the strictly monotone function Z=A^m B^n to classify global limits. For eternal acceleration, construct a semipermeable barrier enclosing a region inside the acceleration domain and trap the exceptional connecting orbit there.
